heading: Overview
text: Communication primitives are the tensor movement operations used by distributed training. Common primitives include broadcast, all-reduce, all-gather, and reduce-scatter.

heading: Core idea
text:
Distributed training uses ranks.

A rank is one process in a communication group.

Ranks exchange tensors with communication primitives.

These operations define how tensors move and combine.

heading: Common primitives
text:
| Primitive | Result |
|---|---|
| broadcast | one rank sends the same tensor to all ranks |
| reduce | many ranks combine tensors on one rank |
| all-reduce | many ranks combine tensors on all ranks |
| scatter | one rank splits a tensor across ranks |
| gather | many ranks send tensors to one rank |
| all-gather | many ranks send tensors to all ranks |
| reduce-scatter | ranks reduce tensors, then scatter shards |
| send and receive | one rank sends to another rank |
| barrier | ranks wait until all ranks arrive |

heading: All-reduce
text:
All-reduce often sums or averages tensors.

If ranks hold $x_1,\dots,x_n$, sum all-reduce gives every rank:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i.
$$

DDP uses all-reduce for gradients.

heading: Reduce-scatter
text:
Reduce-scatter combines reduction and sharding.

FSDP uses reduce-scatter for gradients.

This avoids storing the full reduced tensor on every rank.

heading: Performance notes
text:
Communication cost depends on tensor size, rank count, topology, and bandwidth.

Small messages can suffer from latency.

Large messages can saturate bandwidth.

Good training code overlaps communication with compute when possible.

heading: Overview
text: DDP copies the full model to each rank. Each rank trains on a different batch shard, then ranks all-reduce gradients before the optimizer step.

heading: Core idea
text:
Distributed Data Parallel is the standard data-parallel training method.

Each rank has a full model replica.

Each rank receives a different part of the batch.

The forward and backward pass run locally.

Then DDP averages gradients across ranks with all-reduce.

After that, each rank applies the same optimizer update.

This keeps all model replicas equal.

heading: Global batch size
text:
The global batch size is:

$$
B_{\text{global}}
=
B_{\text{per rank}}
\times
N_{\text{ranks}}
\times
N_{\text{accumulation}}.
$$

See Gradient Accumulation for accumulation steps.

Large global batches can need learning-rate tuning.

heading: Data sharding
text:
Each rank must see a different data shard.

In PyTorch, `DistributedSampler` handles this for map-style datasets.

If all ranks read the same samples, training wastes compute.

heading: Code example
text:
```python

from torch.nn.parallel import DistributedDataParallel as DDP
from torch.utils.data.distributed import DistributedSampler

model = MyModel().cuda()
model = DDP(model, device_ids=[local_rank])

sampler = DistributedSampler(dataset)
loader = DataLoader(dataset, sampler=sampler, batch_size=32)

for x, y in loader:
    loss = loss_fn(model(x.cuda()), y.cuda())
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not forget to shard data.

Do not call the optimizer step before gradients synchronize.

Do not compare DDP speed without communication time.

Use Profiling to find the bottleneck.

heading: Overview
text: Gradients can explode or vanish when backpropagation multiplies many Jacobians. Products with large singular values grow, while products with small singular values shrink.

heading: Core idea
text:
Backpropagation applies the chain rule through many layers or time steps.

For hidden states:

$$
h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t),
$$

a gradient can contain products like:

$$
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t}
=
\prod_{k=t+1}^{T}
\frac{\partial h_k}{\partial h_{k-1}}.
$$

If the Jacobian norms are usually greater than one, gradients can explode.

If they are usually less than one, gradients can vanish.

This problem is common in deep networks and RNNs.

heading: Effects
text:
Exploding gradients can cause unstable loss and `NaN` values.

Vanishing gradients can make early layers learn very slowly.

Saturating activation functions can make vanishing gradients worse.

See Activation Functions.

heading: Fixes
text:
Use careful Weight Initialization.

Use residual connections and normalization layers.

Use gated architectures such as LSTMs.

Use Gradient Clipping for exploding gradients.

Use non-saturating activations when suitable.


Assume each scalar derivative has magnitude $a$.

A chain of $T$ such factors has magnitude:

$$
|a|^T.
$$

If $|a| < 1$, then $|a|^T$ moves toward zero as $T$ grows.

If $|a| > 1$, then $|a|^T$ grows as $T$ grows.

Matrix Jacobian products behave similarly through singular values.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not treat exploding and vanishing gradients as the same failure.

Do not assume clipping fixes vanishing gradients.

Do not ignore initialization and normalization.

heading: Overview
text: Floating point numbers approximate real numbers with fixed bits. They have limited range, limited precision, and rounding error.

heading: Core idea
text:
A floating point number stores three parts:

| Part | Purpose |
|---|---|
| sign | stores positive or negative sign |
| exponent | stores scale |
| significand | stores significant bits |

A simplified value has the form:

$$
(-1)^{s} \times 1.m \times 2^{e}.
$$

The exponent controls range.

The significand controls precision.

heading: Common formats
text:
| Format | Bits | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| fp32 | 32 | common training and optimizer format |
| fp16 | 16 | fast but small exponent range |
| bf16 | 16 | fp32-like exponent range with fewer significand bits |
| fp64 | 64 | high precision but slower on many accelerators |

Mixed Precision Training uses these formats together.

heading: Rounding and non-associativity
text:
Floating point addition is not always associative.

Usually:

$$
(a+b)+c \ne a+(b+c).
$$

This happens because each operation rounds.

Parallel reductions can change summation order.

Thus, distributed runs can produce small numeric differences.

heading: Overflow and underflow
text:
Overflow occurs when a value exceeds the maximum finite value.

Underflow occurs when a value becomes too close to zero.

These failures often appear in exponentials, divisions, and low-precision gradients.

Use Numerical Precision Tricks to reduce risk.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


a = np.float32(1e20)
b = np.float32(-1e20)
c = np.float32(3.14)

print((a + b) + c)
print(a + (b + c))
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not assume floating point math equals real-number math.

Do not assume exact reproducibility across devices.

Do not compare floats with exact equality unless values are controlled.

heading: Overview
text: FSDP is data parallel training with sharded model state. Each rank stores only a shard of parameters, gradients, and optimizer state most of the time.

heading: Core idea
text:
Fully Sharded Data Parallel is a memory-saving form of data parallelism.

Each rank processes a different batch shard.

Unlike DDP, each rank does not keep a full model copy.

FSDP shards three large states:

| State | What FSDP does |
|---|---|
| parameters | shards across ranks |
| gradients | shards after backward |
| optimizer state | shards across ranks |

For a layer, FSDP all-gathers parameter shards before compute.

After backward, FSDP reduce-scatters gradients.

This keeps only local shards between layer computations.

heading: Memory benefit
text:
Adam training can store several values per parameter.

It can store parameters, gradients, first moments, and second moments.

FSDP divides much of this state by the number of ranks.

This helps train large models with limited device memory.

heading: Communication pattern
text:
FSDP uses Communication Primitives heavily.

It all-gathers parameters before a layer runs.

It reduce-scatters gradients after backward.

Overlap between compute and communication is important.

heading: Code example
text:
```python

from torch.distributed.fsdp import FullyShardedDataParallel as FSDP

model = MyModel().cuda()
model = FSDP(model)

for x, y in loader:
    out = model(x.cuda())
    loss = loss_fn(out, y.cuda())
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()
    optimizer.zero_grad()
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not assume FSDP removes all memory cost.

A layer can still need full parameters during its compute.

Do not use too small shard groups without testing.

Extra communication can erase memory gains.

heading: Overview
text: Gradient accumulation runs backward on several microbatches before one optimizer step. It simulates a larger batch with lower peak activation memory.

heading: Core idea
text:
A large batch can exceed device memory.

Gradient accumulation splits it into microbatches.

For each microbatch, the code runs forward and backward.

The optimizer step happens after several backward passes.

The accumulated gradient approximates the gradient of the larger batch.

heading: Loss scaling across microbatches
text:
If the loss function returns a mean over a microbatch, divide the loss by the number of accumulation steps.

This keeps the gradient scale close to the large-batch gradient.

For $A$ accumulation steps:

$$
\ell_{\text{scaled}} = \frac{\ell}{A}.
$$

Without this division, the gradient can become $A$ times larger.

heading: Global batch size
text:
The global batch size is:

$$
B_{\text{global}}
=
B_{\text{micro}}
\times A
\times R.
$$

Here, $R$ is the number of data-parallel ranks.

See DDP.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
accum_steps = 4
optimizer.zero_grad()

for i, (x, y) in enumerate(loader):
    pred = model(x)
    loss = loss_fn(pred, y) / accum_steps
    loss.backward()

    if (i + 1) % accum_steps == 0:
        optimizer.step()
        optimizer.zero_grad()
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not forget to divide the loss.

Do not call `zero_grad` after every microbatch.

Do not confuse microbatch size with global batch size.

heading: Overview
text: Gradient checkpointing stores fewer activations in the forward pass. During backward, it recomputes missing activations to save memory.

heading: Core idea
text:
Backpropagation needs intermediate activations.

Large models can store many activations.

Gradient checkpointing saves only selected activations.

During backward, it reruns parts of the forward pass.

This trades extra compute for lower memory.

heading: Memory and compute tradeoff
text:
Without checkpointing, training stores most activations.

With checkpointing, training stores checkpoints and recomputes the rest.

Peak activation memory can fall a lot.

Step time usually increases because recomputation adds work.

Use Profiling to measure the tradeoff.

heading: When to use it
text:
Use checkpointing when activations limit batch size or sequence length.

It helps transformer models with long sequences.

It combines well with FSDP.

It does not reduce parameter memory by itself.

heading: Code example
Common mistakes
text:
Do not expect checkpointing to reduce all memory.

It mainly reduces activation memory.

Do not checkpoint tiny operations.

The recompute overhead can dominate.

heading: Overview
text: Gradient clipping limits the size of gradients before the optimizer step. It helps when gradients explode and cause unstable updates.

heading: Core idea
text:
Gradient clipping changes gradients when they exceed a threshold.

The most common method clips the global norm.

Let $g$ be the vector of all gradients.

Let $c$ be the maximum norm.

If $\lVert g\rVert_2 > c$, replace $g$ with:

$$
g_{\text{clipped}}
=
g \frac{c}{\lVert g\rVert_2 + \epsilon}.
$$

If $\lVert g\rVert_2 \le c$, keep $g$ unchanged.

heading: Why it helps
text:
Large gradients can create very large optimizer steps.

This can destabilize training.

Gradient clipping is common in RNNs, transformers, and reinforcement learning.

It directly helps Exploding and Vanishing Gradients.

heading: Norm clipping vs value clipping
text:
Norm clipping preserves the gradient direction unless clipping occurs.

Value clipping clips each gradient element separately.

Value clipping can change direction more strongly.

Norm clipping is usually the default choice.


Assume $\lVert g\rVert_2 > c$.

The clipped gradient is:

$$
g_{\text{clipped}}
=
\alpha g,
\quad
\alpha =
\frac{c}{\lVert g\rVert_2+\epsilon}.
$$

The scalar $\alpha$ is positive.

Multiplying a vector by a positive scalar keeps its direction.

Thus, norm clipping reduces magnitude but keeps direction.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
loss.backward()

torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(
    model.parameters(),
    max_norm=1.0,
)

optimizer.step()
optimizer.zero_grad()
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not use clipping to hide a broken loss.

Do not clip after the optimizer step.

Do not choose a threshold without monitoring gradient norms.

heading: Overview
text: JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow all support tensors, autodiff, and accelerators. They differ in programming style, compiler model, and ecosystem.

heading: Core idea
text:
A tensor framework provides arrays, automatic differentiation, neural-network layers, and accelerator execution.

The three common frameworks are JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow.

All three can train large models.

All three can use GPUs and TPUs, with different support levels.

heading: PyTorch
text:
PyTorch uses eager execution by default.

This makes debugging direct and Python-like.

PyTorch also has `torch.compile` for graph capture and compilation.

PyTorch has strong support for research code and distributed training.

See DDP and FSDP.

heading: JAX
text:
JAX uses function transformations.

Important transformations include `grad`, `jit`, `vmap`, and `pmap`.

JAX code usually works best with pure functions and immutable arrays.

JAX integrates closely with XLA compilation.

See JIT Compiling.

heading: TensorFlow
text:
TensorFlow supports eager execution and graph execution.

`tf.function` converts Python functions into TensorFlow graphs.

Keras provides a high-level model API.

TensorFlow has production tools such as TensorFlow Serving and TensorFlow Lite.

heading: Choosing a framework
text:
Choose based on team skill, ecosystem, deployment target, and distributed needs.

Use Profiling before making performance claims.

Small examples can mislead because compiler warmup and input pipelines matter.

heading: Code comparison
text:
```python
# PyTorch gradient
x = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
y = x * x
y.backward()
print(x.grad)

# JAX gradient
grad_fn = jax.grad(lambda z: z * z)
print(grad_fn(2.0))
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not assume one framework is always fastest.

Do not compare eager code in one framework with compiled code in another.

Do not ignore deployment and debugging needs.

heading: Overview
text: JIT compiling captures tensor code and compiles it into faster kernels or graphs. The first call can compile, while later calls reuse the compiled plan.

heading: Core idea
text:
JIT means just-in-time.

A JIT compiler runs during program execution.

It traces or stages tensor operations.

Then it builds an optimized graph or kernel plan.

This can reduce Python overhead and fuse operations.

JAX uses `jax.jit`.

PyTorch uses `torch.compile`.

TensorFlow uses `tf.function`.

See JAX, PyTorch, TensorFlow.

heading: Static shapes and recompilation
text:
Compilers often specialize to shapes and data types.

A new shape can trigger a new compilation.

Frequent recompilation can make code slower.

Batch shapes should stay stable when possible.

heading: Control flow
text:
Python control flow can be hard to trace.

Frameworks provide graph-friendly control flow tools.

In JAX, use `jax.lax` for many compiled control-flow patterns.

In TensorFlow, AutoGraph can convert some Python control flow.

heading: Code example
Common mistakes
text:
Do not benchmark only the first compiled call.

The first call can include compilation time.

Do not change shapes every step.

Do not put side effects inside compiled functions.

heading: Overview
text: Mixed precision training uses fp16 or bf16 for many operations. It keeps sensitive values in fp32 when stability needs it.

heading: Core idea
text:
Lower precision can reduce memory and improve throughput.

Common formats include fp16 and bf16.

Many accelerators have fast matrix kernels for these formats.

Training still needs care because gradients can underflow or overflow.

Mixed precision usually keeps some operations in fp32.

Examples include loss accumulation, optimizer state, and some reductions.

heading: fp16 and bf16
text:
fp16 has limited exponent range.

It often needs loss scaling.

bf16 has the same exponent size as fp32.

It has fewer mantissa bits than fp32.

bf16 usually handles large and small values better than fp16.

See Floating Point Representation.

heading: Loss scaling
text:
Loss scaling multiplies the loss before backward.

This makes small fp16 gradients larger during computation.

After backward, the scaler divides gradients before the optimizer step.

Dynamic loss scaling changes the scale when overflow appears.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


scaler = torch.cuda.amp.GradScaler()

for x, y in loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()

    with torch.cuda.amp.autocast(dtype=torch.float16):
        pred = model(x.cuda())
        loss = loss_fn(pred, y.cuda())

    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not cast every operation to fp16.

Softmax, normalization, and reductions can need fp32.

Do not use fp16 loss scaling rules for every bf16 run.

bf16 often does not need loss scaling.

heading: Overview
text: Numerical precision tricks avoid overflow, underflow, and cancellation. Common tricks include log-sum-exp, stable softmax, epsilons, and fp32 accumulation.

heading: Core idea
text:
Floating point arithmetic has finite range and finite precision.

Naive formulas can overflow, underflow, or lose small differences.

Stable formulas compute the same mathematical value in a safer way.

See Floating Point Representation.

heading: Stable softmax
text:
Naive softmax computes:

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(x_i)
=
\frac{\exp(x_i)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j)}.
$$

Large $x_i$ can make $\exp(x_i)$ overflow.

Subtract the maximum logit $m=\max_j x_j$:

$$
\operatorname{softmax}(x_i)
=
\frac{\exp(x_i-m)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j-m)}.
$$

This gives the same result and avoids large exponentials.


Let $c$ be any constant.

$$
\frac{\exp(x_i-c)}{\sum_j \exp(x_j-c)}
=
\frac{\exp(x_i)\exp(-c)}
{\sum_j \exp(x_j)\exp(-c)}.
$$

The factor $\exp(-c)$ appears in the numerator and denominator.

It cancels out.

Thus, subtracting $c$ does not change softmax.

heading: Log-sum-exp
text:
Use:

$$
\log \sum_i \exp(x_i)
=
m + \log \sum_i \exp(x_i-m).
$$

This is stable when $m=\max_i x_i$.

heading: Other tricks
text:
Add a small $\epsilon$ before division or logarithms.

Use `log1p(x)` for $\log(1+x)$ when $x$ is small.

Use `expm1(x)` for $\exp(x)-1$ when $x$ is small.

Accumulate reductions in fp32 during Mixed Precision Training.

heading: Code example
Common mistakes
text:
Do not compute softmax before cross entropy if the library expects logits.

Do not take `log(softmax(x))` manually.

Use a fused stable cross-entropy function when possible.

heading: Overview
text: Pipeline parallelism splits a model by layers. Devices process microbatches in a schedule so multiple stages work at the same time.

heading: Core idea
text:
Pipeline parallelism partitions a model into sequential stages.

Each stage runs on a different device or device group.

Stage 1 sends activations to stage 2.

During backward, stage 2 sends activation gradients back to stage 1.

A large batch is split into microbatches.

Microbatches keep pipeline stages busy.

heading: Pipeline bubble
text:
At the start and end of a batch, some stages sit idle.

This idle time is the pipeline bubble.

For $p$ stages and $m$ microbatches, a simple bubble fraction is:

$$
\frac{p - 1}{m + p - 1}.
$$

More microbatches reduce the bubble.

Too many microbatches can increase overhead.

heading: Schedules
text:
GPipe runs all forward microbatches before backward microbatches.

A 1F1B schedule alternates one forward and one backward after warmup.

1F1B often reduces activation memory.

heading: Communication
text:
Pipeline stages communicate activations and gradients.

This uses send and receive operations.

See Communication Primitives.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not split layers without checking balance.

The slowest stage limits throughput.

Do not ignore activation memory.

Do not use too few microbatches.

heading: Overview
text: Profiling measures where time and memory go. It helps separate compute bottlenecks, memory bottlenecks, input bottlenecks, and communication bottlenecks.

heading: Core idea
text:
Do not optimize before you measure.

A profiler records operations, duration, memory use, and device activity.

Common tools include PyTorch Profiler, TensorBoard, Nsight Systems, and framework logs.

Profiling answers questions such as:

| Question | Signal |
|---|---|
| Is the GPU idle? | input pipeline or synchronization problem |
| Are kernels small? | launch overhead or fragmentation |
| Is memory near full? | activation, parameter, or optimizer memory |
| Is all-reduce slow? | communication bottleneck |

heading: GPU timing
text:
GPU operations are often asynchronous.

A CPU timer can finish before GPU work finishes.

Use device synchronization around simple timers.

```python



torch.cuda.synchronize()
t0 = time.time()

loss = model(x).sum()
loss.backward()

torch.cuda.synchronize()
print(time.time() - t0)
```

heading: Profiling loop
text:
A good profiling loop has warmup steps and measured steps.

Warmup avoids one-time costs.

This matters for JIT Compiling and kernel caching.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not trust a single step.

Do not include data download time unless you want to measure it.

Do not ignore synchronization.

Do not optimize the largest-looking operation without checking end-to-end time.

heading: Overview
text: Tensor parallelism splits one large layer across devices. Each device computes part of the tensor operation, then devices communicate partial results.

heading: Core idea
text:
Large models often contain weight matrices that do not fit well on one device.

Tensor parallelism partitions these matrices across devices.

For a linear layer:

$$
Y = XW.
$$

A column split partitions the output columns:

$$
W = [W_1, W_2, \dots, W_k].
$$

Each device computes:

$$
Y_i = XW_i.
$$

Then the system concatenates the outputs:

$$
Y = [Y_1, Y_2, \dots, Y_k].
$$

A row split partitions the input dimension:

$$
W =
\begin{bmatrix}
W_1 \\
W_2 \\
\vdots \\
W_k
\end{bmatrix},
\quad
X = [X_1, X_2, \dots, X_k].
$$

Each device computes a partial output:

$$
Z_i = X_iW_i.
$$

Then devices use an all-reduce sum:

$$
Y = \sum_i Z_i.
$$

See Communication Primitives for all-reduce and all-gather.

heading: Where it helps
text:
Tensor parallelism helps when one layer is too large or too slow for one device.

It often appears in transformer MLP layers and attention projections.

It can combine with Pipeline Parallelism and DDP.

heading: Communication cost
text:
Tensor parallelism reduces local work.

It adds communication inside a layer.

The best split depends on tensor shape, network speed, and kernel support.

Small layers can become slower because communication dominates compute.

heading: Code sketch
text:
```python


x = torch.randn(8, 4096)
w = torch.randn(4096, 8192)

# Column split across two devices or ranks.
w1, w2 = torch.chunk(w, chunks=2, dim=1)

y1 = x @ w1
y2 = x @ w2

y = torch.cat([y1, y2], dim=1)
print(y.shape)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not confuse tensor parallelism with data parallelism.

Tensor parallelism splits one layer.

Data parallelism copies the model and splits the batch.

Do not ignore collective communication.

The communication pattern often decides the speed.

heading: Overview
text: Activation functions make neural networks nonlinear. Their derivatives strongly affect training.

heading: Core idea
text:
Without nonlinear activations, stacked linear layers reduce to one linear map.

An activation function applies after a layer output:

$$
a=\phi(z).
$$

Common activations include ReLU, sigmoid, tanh, GELU, and SiLU.

heading: ReLU
text:
ReLU is:

$$
\operatorname{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z).
$$

Its derivative is:

$$
\operatorname{ReLU}'(z)=
\begin{cases}
1 & z>0 \\
0 & z<0
\end{cases}
$$

ReLU is cheap and reduces saturation for positive inputs.

heading: Sigmoid and tanh
text:
Sigmoid maps values to $(0,1)$:

$$
\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-z)}.
$$

Tanh maps values to $(-1,1)$.

Both can saturate for large absolute inputs.

Saturation can cause small gradients.

heading: GELU and SiLU
text:
GELU and SiLU are smooth activations.

They are common in large neural networks.

GELU roughly keeps an input with probability based on its value.

heading: Code example
Common mistakes
text:
Do not use a final sigmoid before a logits-based binary cross-entropy loss.

Do not use sigmoid in every hidden layer by default.

Do not ignore activation and initialization together.

heading: Overview
text: Adaptive optimizers scale updates with gradient history. Adam uses first and second moments. AdamW decouples weight decay from Adam.

heading: Adagrad
text:
Adagrad accumulates squared gradients:

$$
G_t = G_{t-1}+g_t^2.
$$

The update is:

$$
\theta_{t+1}
=
\theta_t
-
\eta \frac{g_t}{\sqrt{G_t}+\epsilon}.
$$

Parameters with large past gradients get smaller steps.

heading: Adam
text:
Adam tracks an exponential average of gradients:

$$
m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t.
$$

It also tracks squared gradients:

$$
v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2.
$$

With bias correction:

$$
\hat m_t=\frac{m_t}{1-\beta_1^t},
\quad
\hat v_t=\frac{v_t}{1-\beta_2^t}.
$$

The update is:

$$
\theta_{t+1}
=
\theta_t-\eta\frac{\hat m_t}{\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\epsilon}.
$$

heading: AdamW
text:
AdamW decouples weight decay from the adaptive gradient step.

This often works better than L2 regularization inside Adam.

See Regularization Methods.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * g
v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * (g * g)

m_hat = m / (1 - beta1 ** t)
v_hat = v / (1 - beta2 ** t)

theta = theta - lr * m_hat / (np.sqrt(v_hat) + eps)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not omit epsilon in the denominator.

Do not confuse AdamW with Adam plus L2 penalty.

Do not compare optimizers without learning-rate tuning.

heading: Overview
text: An autoencoder pairs an encoder $z=f(x)$ with a decoder $\hat{x}=g(z)$ and minimizes reconstruction error. A linear autoencoder with squared loss recovers the PCA subspace. Denoising, sparse, and contractive variants add constraints so that the code captures structure rather than identity.

heading: Basic form
text:
$$
z = f_\theta(x),
\qquad
\hat{x} = g_\phi(z),
\qquad
\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|x_i - g_\phi(f_\theta(x_i))\|^2 .
$$

The code $z$ has lower dimension than $x$ in the undercomplete case. That bottleneck forces the network to keep only what matters for reconstruction.

The training signal comes from the input itself, so no labels are needed.

heading: Relation to PCA
text:
Let the encoder and decoder be linear with no bias, so $z = Wx$ and $\hat{x} = Vz = VWx$, with $W \in \mathbb{R}^{k\times d}$ and $V\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}$.

Assume the data is centered. The objective is

$$
\min_{V,W}\ \mathbb{E}\big[\|x - VWx\|^2\big].
$$

Let $M = VW$. Since $V$ and $W$ have inner dimension $k$, the matrix $M$ has rank at most $k$. Any rank $k$ matrix can be factored this way, so the problem is

$$
\min_{\operatorname{rank}(M)\le k}\ \mathbb{E}\big[\|x - Mx\|^2\big].
$$

Write the objective with the covariance $\Sigma = \mathbb{E}[xx^\top]$:

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\|(I-M)x\|^2\big]
=
\operatorname{tr}\big((I-M)\Sigma(I-M)^\top\big).
$$

By the Eckart-Young theorem, the best rank $k$ approximation in this sense is the orthogonal projection onto the span of the top $k$ eigenvectors of $\Sigma$. So

$$
M^\star = U_k U_k^\top ,
$$

where $U_k$ holds the top $k$ eigenvectors.

Therefore the optimal $W$ has row space equal to the top $k$ principal subspace. The individual rows need not be the principal components, because any invertible $k\times k$ change of basis $R$ gives the same product through $W' = RW$ and $V' = VR^{-1}$.


So a linear autoencoder finds the same subspace as PCA but not the same axes. Nonlinear encoders can capture curved manifolds that PCA cannot.

heading: Denoising autoencoder
text:
Corrupt the input, then ask for the clean target:

$$
\tilde{x} \sim q(\tilde{x}\mid x),
\qquad
\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}\big[\|x - g(f(\tilde{x}))\|^2\big].
$$

Common corruptions are additive Gaussian noise, random masking, and dropout on the input.

The model cannot copy the input, so it must learn the data structure that lets it fill in missing parts. A denoising autoencoder with small Gaussian noise learns a function proportional to the score $\nabla_x \log p(x)$, which links it to diffusion models.

Masked prediction in modern pretraining is a denoising autoencoder with token masking.

heading: Sparse autoencoder
text:
Add a penalty that keeps most code units near zero:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \|x-\hat{x}\|^2 + \lambda\|z\|_1 ,
$$

or a KL penalty toward a small target activation $\rho$:

$$
\sum_{j}\rho\log\frac{\rho}{\hat{\rho}_j} + (1-\rho)\log\frac{1-\rho}{1-\hat{\rho}_j}.
$$

Sparsity allows an overcomplete code, where $\dim(z) > \dim(x)$, without collapsing to the identity. Sparse autoencoders are now widely used to find interpretable features inside language model activations.

heading: Contractive autoencoder
text:
Penalize the sensitivity of the code to input changes:

$$
\mathcal{L} = \|x-\hat{x}\|^2 + \lambda\left\|\frac{\partial f(x)}{\partial x}\right\|_F^2 .
$$

The Jacobian penalty makes the representation flat in directions that leave the data manifold and responsive along the manifold.

heading: Variational autoencoder
text:
A VAE is a generative model, not just a compressor. The encoder outputs a distribution $q_\phi(z\mid x)$ and the objective is the evidence lower bound:

$$
\mathcal{L}_{\text{ELBO}}
=
\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)\big]
- D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big).
$$

The KL term regularizes the latent space so that sampling from the prior produces valid outputs. A plain autoencoder has no such guarantee and its latent space contains holes.

heading: Uses and limits
text:
| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| Nonlinear dimensionality reduction | Parametric, applies to new points |
| Anomaly detection | Flag high reconstruction error |
| Denoising and inpainting | Direct application of the training task |
| Pretraining | Masked autoencoders for vision and text |
| Discrete codes | VQ-VAE for tokenizing images and audio |

Limits:

- A plain autoencoder can learn a near identity map if the capacity is too large.
- Reconstruction error is not the same as usefulness for a downstream task.
- Squared loss produces blurry image outputs.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


def linear_ae_grads(X, W, V):
    """Squared reconstruction loss for z = W x, xhat = V z."""
    Z = X @ W.T
    Xh = Z @ V.T
    E = Xh - X
    n = len(X)
    loss = np.mean(np.sum(E ** 2, axis=1))
    gV = 2.0 / n * E.T @ Z
    gW = 2.0 / n * (E @ V).T @ X
    return loss, gW, gV

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
base = rng.normal(size=(400, 2))
X = base @ rng.normal(size=(2, 8))
X = X - X.mean(0)

W = rng.normal(size=(2, 8)) * 0.1
V = rng.normal(size=(8, 2)) * 0.1
for step in range(3000):
    loss, gW, gV = linear_ae_grads(X, W, V)
    W -= 0.01 * gW
    V -= 0.01 * gV
print(round(float(loss), 6))
```

The loss should approach zero, because the data has rank two and the code has size two.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not give a plain autoencoder a bottleneck as large as the input without a regularizer. It will learn the identity.

Do not treat a plain autoencoder latent space as a generative prior. Use a VAE for that.

Do not compare reconstruction losses across models with different input scaling.

heading: Overview
text: Backpropagation computes gradients from outputs back to inputs. It reuses intermediate derivatives with the chain rule.

heading: Core idea
text:
A neural network is a composition of functions.

$$
y = f_3(f_2(f_1(x))).
$$

Backpropagation computes:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta}
$$

for each parameter $\theta$.

It does this from the loss backward through the graph.

heading: Chain rule
text:
For scalar functions:

$$
\frac{dL}{dx}
=
\frac{dL}{dz}\frac{dz}{dx}.
$$

For vector functions, use Jacobians.

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}
=
\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}.
$$

See Jacobian.

heading: Linear layer
text:
For a linear layer:

$$
z = xW + b.
$$

Given upstream gradient $g_z=\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}$:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial W}=x^\top g_z,
$$

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial b}=g_z,
$$

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}=g_z W^\top.
$$

heading: Activation layer
text:
For an elementwise activation:

$$
a=\phi(z).
$$

The backward rule is:

$$
g_z = g_a \odot \phi'(z).
$$

Use Activation Functions for common derivatives.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
# Forward
z = x @ W + b
a = np.maximum(z, 0.0)
loss = np.mean((a - y) ** 2)

# Backward for ReLU and MSE
g_a = 2 * (a - y) / y.size
g_z = g_a * (z > 0)
g_W = x.T @ g_z
g_b = g_z.sum(axis=0)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not recompute all derivatives independently.

Do not forget matrix shapes.

Do not update parameters before all gradients are computed.
```

heading: Overview
text: Bagging draws bootstrap samples, fits one base model per sample, and averages the predictions. Averaging reduces variance but leaves bias almost unchanged, so it suits unstable low bias learners such as deep trees. Random forests add feature subsampling to lower the correlation between trees.

heading: Algorithm
text:
1. For $b = 1,\dots,B$, draw a bootstrap sample of size $n$ from the training set with replacement.
2. Fit a base model $\hat{f}_b$ on that sample.
3. Average for regression, or vote for classification:

$$
\hat{f}_{\mathrm{bag}}(x) = \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat{f}_b(x).
$$

The models train independently, so bagging parallelizes perfectly.

heading: Why averaging reduces variance
text:
Let $\hat{f}_1,\dots,\hat{f}_B$ each have variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$.

The variance of the average is

$$
\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\hat{f}_b\right)
=
\frac{1}{B^2}\left[\sum_b \operatorname{Var}(\hat{f}_b)
+ \sum_{b \neq b'}\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{f}_b,\hat{f}_{b'})\right].
$$

There are $B$ variance terms and $B(B-1)$ covariance terms. Each covariance equals $\rho\sigma^2$:

$$
=
\frac{1}{B^2}\big[B\sigma^2 + B(B-1)\rho\sigma^2\big].
$$

Simplify:

$$
=
\rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2 .
$$

As $B\to\infty$ the second term vanishes and the variance approaches $\rho\sigma^2$.


Two lessons follow.

1. More models help, but the benefit saturates at $\rho\sigma^2$.
2. Reducing the correlation $\rho$ matters more than adding models once $B$ is large.

heading: Bias stays the same
text:
Each bootstrap model estimates roughly the same function. So

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{f}_{\mathrm{bag}}(x)\big]
\approx
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat{f}_b(x)\big].
$$

Bagging therefore does not reduce bias. Use a low bias, high variance base learner such as a fully grown decision tree.

Bagging a linear model gives almost no gain, because linear fits are already stable.

heading: Out-of-bag estimate
text:
A bootstrap sample omits some training points.

The probability that a given point is missing from one bootstrap sample is

$$
\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)^n \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{} e^{-1} \approx 0.368 .
$$

So about 36.8 percent of points are out-of-bag for each model.

Predict each training point using only the models that did not see it. The resulting out-of-bag error estimates generalization without a separate validation split. It behaves much like cross validation at no extra training cost.

heading: Random forests
text:
A random forest is bagging plus a second source of randomness. At each split the tree considers only a random subset of `max_features` features.

This lowers $\rho$ between trees, so the variance floor $\rho\sigma^2$ drops.

| Setting | Typical value |
|---|---|
| `max_features` for classification | $\sqrt{d}$ |
| `max_features` for regression | $d/3$ |
| `n_estimators` | As many as compute allows |
| `max_depth` | Unlimited or very deep |

More trees never overfit a random forest. They only reduce variance. Depth and feature count control the fit.

Extremely randomized trees push this further. They pick split thresholds at random, which lowers correlation and variance again at a small cost in bias.

heading: Bagging compared with boosting
text:
| Aspect | Bagging | Boosting |
|---|---|---|
| Base learner | Low bias, high variance | High bias, low variance |
| Training | Parallel | Sequential |
| Reduces | Variance | Bias, then variance |
| Overfits with more models | No | Yes |
| Sample weights | Uniform bootstrap | Reweighted by errors |

heading: Code example
text:
```python

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

def bagging_fit(X, y, B=50, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = len(X)
    models, oob_masks = [], []
    for _ in range(B):
        idx = rng.integers(0, n, size=n)
        mask = np.ones(n, dtype=bool)
        mask[np.unique(idx)] = False
        model = DecisionTreeRegressor().fit(X[idx], y[idx])
        models.append(model)
        oob_masks.append(mask)
    return models, oob_masks

def bagging_predict(models, X):
    return np.mean([m.predict(X) for m in models], axis=0)

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(300, 5))
y = X[:, 0] ** 2 + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=300)
models, _ = bagging_fit(X, y)
pred = bagging_predict(models, X)
print(np.mean((pred - y) ** 2))
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not bag a high bias model and expect a gain.

Do not sample without replacement and call it bagging. Sampling without replacement is pasting.

Do not treat out-of-bag error as a test score after you tune hyperparameters on it. It then becomes a validation score.

heading: Overview
text: Bayes' theorem converts a prior and a likelihood into a posterior. It gives a precise rule for belief updates under uncertainty.

heading: Core idea
text:
Bayes' theorem states:

$$
p(A \mid B)
=
\frac{p(B \mid A)p(A)}{p(B)}.
$$

The terms have common names.

| Term | Name |
|---|---|
| $p(A)$ | prior |
| $p(B \mid A)$ | likelihood |
| $p(B)$ | evidence |
| $p(A \mid B)$ | posterior |

The posterior is proportional to likelihood times prior.

$$
p(A \mid B) \propto p(B \mid A)p(A).
$$

heading: Derivation
text:
Bayes' theorem comes from the product rule.

$$
p(A,B)=p(A \mid B)p(B)
$$

and

$$
p(A,B)=p(B \mid A)p(A).
$$

Equate the two expressions:

$$
p(A \mid B)p(B)
=
p(B \mid A)p(A).
$$

Then divide by $p(B)$.

The product rule gives:

$$
p(A,B)=p(A \mid B)p(B).
$$

It also gives:

$$
p(A,B)=p(B \mid A)p(A).
$$

Both expressions equal the same joint probability.

Therefore:

$$
p(A \mid B)p(B)=p(B \mid A)p(A).
$$

When $p(B)>0$:

$$
p(A \mid B)=\frac{p(B \mid A)p(A)}{p(B)}.
$$

heading: Evidence as normalization
text:
For a set of mutually exclusive cases $A_1,\dots,A_k$:

$$
p(B)
=
\sum_i p(B \mid A_i)p(A_i).
$$

This makes the posterior probabilities sum to one.

For continuous parameters $\theta$:

$$
p(\theta \mid x)
=
\frac{p(x \mid \theta)p(\theta)}
{\int p(x \mid \theta)p(\theta)\,d\theta}.
$$

Use PDF and PMF to track discrete and continuous cases.

heading: Base rates
text:
Base rates can strongly affect the posterior.

A rare condition can still have low posterior probability after a positive test.

This happens when false positives are not rare enough.

heading: MAP estimation
text:
Maximum a posteriori estimation chooses the parameter with largest posterior.

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}
=
\arg\max_\theta p(\theta \mid x).
$$

Since the evidence does not depend on $\theta$:

$$
\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}
=
\arg\max_\theta p(x \mid \theta)p(\theta).
$$

See MLE vs MAP for the link to optimization.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
prior = 0.01
sensitivity = 0.99
false_positive_rate = 0.05

evidence = sensitivity * prior + false_positive_rate * (1 - prior)
posterior = sensitivity * prior / evidence

print(posterior)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not ignore the prior.

Do not confuse $p(A \mid B)$ with $p(B \mid A)$.

Do not forget the evidence term.

heading: Overview
text: Bias is systematic error from a restricted model. Variance is error from sensitivity to the training sample. Noise is irreducible error in the data.

heading: Core idea
text:
Assume the data has this form:

$$
y = f(x) + \epsilon,
$$

where:

$$
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon]=0,
\quad
\operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=\sigma^2.
$$

For squared loss, expected test error decomposes into:

$$
\mathbb{E}[(y-\hat f(x))^2]
=
\operatorname{Bias}[\hat f(x)]^2
+
\operatorname{Var}[\hat f(x)]
+
\sigma^2.
$$

Use Variance and Covariance for the variance term.

heading: Bias
text:
Bias measures systematic error.

$$
\operatorname{Bias}[\hat f(x)]
=
\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)] - f(x).
$$

High bias often means underfitting.

A very simple model can have high bias because it cannot represent the true pattern.

heading: Variance
text:
Variance measures sample sensitivity.

$$
\operatorname{Var}[\hat f(x)]
=
\mathbb{E}\left[
(\hat f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)])^2
\right].
$$

High variance often means overfitting.

A very flexible model can change a lot when the training data changes.

See Overfitting and Underfitting.

heading: Proof
text:
Start with the prediction error:

$$
y-\hat f(x)=f(x)+\epsilon-\hat f(x).
$$

Add and subtract $\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)]$:

$$
y-\hat f(x)
=
f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)]
+
\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)]-\hat f(x)
+
\epsilon.
$$

Square and take expectation.

The cross terms vanish under the usual assumptions.

This gives:

$$
\mathbb{E}[(y-\hat f(x))^2]
=
(\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)]-f(x))^2
+
\mathbb{E}[(\hat f(x)-\mathbb{E}[\hat f(x)])^2]
+
\mathbb{E}[\epsilon^2].
$$

Thus:

$$
\mathbb{E}[(y-\hat f(x))^2]
=
\operatorname{Bias}^2
+
\operatorname{Var}
+
\sigma^2.
$$

heading: Common controls
text:
More data usually reduces variance.

Regularization can reduce variance but can increase bias.

Cross-validation helps select a useful tradeoff.

See Regularization Methods and Cross-Validation.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

model = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=3, random_state=0)
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring="neg_mean_squared_error")
mse = -scores.mean()
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not equate training error with test error.

Do not call noise bias or variance.

Do not assume a larger model always improves test error.

heading: Overview
text: Boosting builds an additive model one weak learner at a time. AdaBoost reweights misclassified examples. Gradient boosting fits each new tree to the negative gradient of the loss. Boosting cuts bias, so more rounds can overfit.

heading: Additive model
text:
Boosting produces

$$
F_M(x) = \sum_{m=1}^{M}\nu\, h_m(x),
$$

where each $h_m$ is a weak learner and $\nu$ is the learning rate. A weak learner performs only slightly better than chance. A depth 2 to 8 tree is the usual choice.

heading: AdaBoost
text:
AdaBoost handles binary labels $y_i \in \{-1,+1\}$.

1. Initialize weights $w_i = 1/n$.
2. For $m = 1,\dots,M$:
   - Fit $h_m$ on the weighted data.
   - Compute the weighted error $\epsilon_m = \sum_i w_i \mathbb{1}[h_m(x_i)\neq y_i]$.
   - Set $\alpha_m = \tfrac{1}{2}\log\frac{1-\epsilon_m}{\epsilon_m}$.
   - Update $w_i \leftarrow w_i \exp(-\alpha_m y_i h_m(x_i))$ and renormalize.
3. Predict $\operatorname{sign}\left(\sum_m \alpha_m h_m(x)\right)$.


AdaBoost performs forward stagewise minimization of the exponential loss

$$
L(F) = \sum_{i=1}^{n}\exp\big(-y_i F(x_i)\big).
$$

Suppose the current model is $F_{m-1}$. Add a term $\alpha h$:

$$
L(\alpha, h)
=
\sum_i \exp\big(-y_i F_{m-1}(x_i)\big)\exp\big(-\alpha y_i h(x_i)\big).
$$

Define the weights $w_i = \exp(-y_i F_{m-1}(x_i))$. Since $y_i h(x_i) \in \{-1,+1\}$,

$$
L(\alpha,h)
=
e^{-\alpha}\sum_{i:\,h(x_i)=y_i} w_i
+
e^{\alpha}\sum_{i:\,h(x_i)\neq y_i} w_i .
$$

Let $\epsilon = \frac{\sum_{i: h(x_i)\neq y_i} w_i}{\sum_i w_i}$ be the normalized weighted error. Divide by $\sum_i w_i$:

$$
\tilde{L}(\alpha)
=
e^{-\alpha}(1-\epsilon) + e^{\alpha}\epsilon .
$$

Differentiate with respect to $\alpha$:

$$
\frac{d\tilde{L}}{d\alpha}
=
-e^{-\alpha}(1-\epsilon) + e^{\alpha}\epsilon = 0 .
$$

So

$$
e^{2\alpha} = \frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon},
\qquad
\alpha = \tfrac{1}{2}\log\frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon}.
$$

The weight update $w_i \leftarrow w_i e^{-\alpha y_i h(x_i)}$ is exactly the new value of $\exp(-y_i F_m(x_i))$ up to a constant. This proves the algorithm.


Note that $\alpha_m$ is positive when $\epsilon_m < 0.5$ and grows as the error falls.

heading: Gradient boosting
text:
Gradient boosting generalizes the idea to any differentiable loss $\ell$.

Treat the ensemble output $F(x_i)$ as a parameter. Perform gradient descent in function space.

1. Initialize $F_0(x) = \arg\min_c \sum_i \ell(y_i, c)$.
2. For $m=1,\dots,M$:
   - Compute pseudo-residuals

     $$
     r_{im} = -\left[\frac{\partial \ell(y_i, F(x_i))}{\partial F(x_i)}\right]_{F=F_{m-1}} .
     $$

   - Fit a regression tree $h_m$ to the pairs $(x_i, r_{im})$.
   - Set the leaf values by a line search on the loss.
   - Update $F_m = F_{m-1} + \nu h_m$.

For squared loss $\ell = \tfrac{1}{2}(y-F)^2$, the pseudo-residual is exactly $y_i - F_{m-1}(x_i)$. Each tree then fits the current residual.

| Loss | Pseudo-residual |
|---|---|
| Squared error | $y_i - F(x_i)$ |
| Absolute error | $\operatorname{sign}(y_i - F(x_i))$ |
| Logistic (binary) | $y_i - \sigma(F(x_i))$ |
| Exponential | Recovers AdaBoost |

heading: Second order boosting
text:
XGBoost uses a second order expansion. For each example define

$$
g_i = \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial F(x_i)},
\qquad
h_i = \frac{\partial^2 \ell}{\partial F(x_i)^2}.
$$

The regularized objective for one tree with leaves $j$ and leaf values $w_j$ is

$$
\mathcal{L}
=
\sum_j \left[\left(\sum_{i\in I_j} g_i\right)w_j
+ \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{i\in I_j} h_i + \lambda\right)w_j^2\right]
+ \gamma T .
$$

Minimize over $w_j$:

$$
w_j^\star = -\frac{\sum_{i\in I_j} g_i}{\sum_{i\in I_j} h_i + \lambda},
$$

and the resulting leaf score is

$$
-\tfrac{1}{2}\frac{\left(\sum_{i\in I_j} g_i\right)^2}{\sum_{i\in I_j} h_i + \lambda}.
$$

The split gain compares the parent score with the sum of the two child scores minus $\gamma$. A split with a negative gain is rejected.

heading: Regularization
text:
| Control | Effect |
|---|---|
| Learning rate $\nu$ | Shrinks each step. Small $\nu$ needs more rounds and generalizes better |
| Number of rounds $M$ | Main capacity dial. Use early stopping |
| Tree depth | Limits interaction order |
| Subsample rows | Stochastic gradient boosting, adds variance reduction |
| Subsample columns | Reduces correlation between trees |
| $\lambda$ and $\gamma$ | L2 on leaf values and per leaf penalty |
| `min_child_weight` | Requires enough Hessian mass per leaf |

A common rule sets $\nu$ around 0.05 and picks $M$ by early stopping on a validation set.

heading: Boosting versus bagging
text:
| Aspect | Boosting | Bagging |
|---|---|---|
| Base learner | Weak, high bias | Strong, high variance |
| Order | Sequential | Parallel |
| Main effect | Reduces bias | Reduces variance |
| More models | Can overfit | Cannot overfit |
| Noise robustness | Lower, AdaBoost chases outliers | Higher |

heading: Code example
text:
```python

from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor

def gradient_boost(X, y, rounds=100, lr=0.1, depth=3):
    F = np.full(len(y), y.mean())
    trees = []
    for _ in range(rounds):
        residual = y - F              # squared loss pseudo-residual
        tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth).fit(X, residual)
        F = F + lr * tree.predict(X)
        trees.append(tree)
    return y.mean(), trees

def gb_predict(base, trees, X, lr=0.1):
    out = np.full(len(X), base)
    for t in trees:
        out += lr * t.predict(X)
    return out

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.normal(size=(400, 4))
y = np.sin(X[:, 0]) + X[:, 1] ** 2 + 0.1 * rng.normal(size=400)
base, trees = gradient_boost(X, y)
print(np.mean((gb_predict(base, trees, X) - y) ** 2))
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not raise the learning rate to save time. Lower the rate and add rounds instead.

Do not fit boosting to heavily mislabeled data without care. AdaBoost gives huge weight to persistent errors.

Do not forget that gradient boosting fits a regression tree even for classification. The tree fits gradients, not classes.

heading: Overview
text: k-means minimizes within cluster squared distance with an alternating assign and update loop. It assumes round, equal sized clusters. GMM adds soft assignment and covariance, DBSCAN finds density based clusters of any shape, and spectral clustering works on a similarity graph.

heading: k-means objective
text:
Given points $x_1,\dots,x_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ and $K$ clusters, minimize

$$
J(\{c_i\},\{\mu_k\})
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\big\|x_i - \mu_{c_i}\big\|^2 ,
$$

over assignments $c_i \in \{1,\dots,K\}$ and centroids $\mu_k$.

This problem is NP-hard in general. Lloyd's algorithm finds a local minimum.

heading: Lloyd's algorithm
text:
1. Initialize $K$ centroids.
2. Assignment step. Set $c_i = \arg\min_k \|x_i - \mu_k\|^2$.
3. Update step. Set $\mu_k$ to the mean of the points assigned to cluster $k$.
4. Repeat steps 2 and 3 until the assignments stop changing.


Write the objective as $J(c, \mu)$.

Assignment step. Fix $\mu$. For each $i$ the term $\|x_i-\mu_{c_i}\|^2$ depends only on $c_i$. Choosing the nearest centroid minimizes that term. So

$$
J(c^{t+1}, \mu^t) \le J(c^t, \mu^t).
$$

Update step. Fix $c$. For cluster $k$ with index set $S_k$, minimize

$$
\sum_{i \in S_k}\|x_i - \mu_k\|^2 .
$$

Take the gradient with respect to $\mu_k$:

$$
-2\sum_{i \in S_k}(x_i - \mu_k) = 0 .
$$

So

$$
\mu_k = \frac{1}{|S_k|}\sum_{i\in S_k} x_i ,
$$

which is the mean. Therefore

$$
J(c^{t+1}, \mu^{t+1}) \le J(c^{t+1}, \mu^t).
$$

Combining both steps, $J$ never increases. The objective is bounded below by zero and the number of distinct assignments is finite. So the algorithm terminates at a local minimum.


Cost per iteration is $O(nKd)$.

heading: k-means++ initialization
text:
Random initialization can give poor local minima. k-means++ spreads the seeds.

1. Pick the first center uniformly at random.
2. For each point compute $D(x)$, the distance to the nearest chosen center.
3. Pick the next center with probability proportional to $D(x)^2$.
4. Repeat until $K$ centers exist.

This gives an expected objective within $O(\log K)$ of the optimum.

heading: Assumptions and failure cases
text:
k-means assumes:

- clusters are roughly spherical in Euclidean distance,
- clusters have similar size and spread,
- the number $K$ is known.

It fails on elongated clusters, nested rings, and very unbalanced sizes. Feature scaling matters, because the distance mixes units.

heading: Gaussian mixture models
text:
A GMM models the density as

$$
p(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{K}\pi_k\,\mathcal{N}(x \mid \mu_k, \Sigma_k).
$$

The EM algorithm alternates two steps.

E step. Compute the responsibility

$$
\gamma_{ik}
=
\frac{\pi_k \mathcal{N}(x_i \mid \mu_k,\Sigma_k)}
{\sum_j \pi_j \mathcal{N}(x_i\mid\mu_j,\Sigma_j)} .
$$

M step. Update

$$
\mu_k = \frac{\sum_i \gamma_{ik}x_i}{\sum_i \gamma_{ik}},
\qquad
\pi_k = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \gamma_{ik},
$$

and the corresponding weighted covariance.

k-means is the limit of a GMM with shared spherical covariance $\sigma^2 I$ as $\sigma^2 \to 0$. Responsibilities then become hard assignments.

heading: DBSCAN
text:
DBSCAN uses two parameters, a radius $\epsilon$ and a minimum count `minPts`.

- A core point has at least `minPts` neighbors within $\epsilon$.
- Points that are density reachable from a core point join the same cluster.
- Points that reach no core point become noise.

Strengths: it finds clusters of any shape, needs no $K$, and labels outliers.

Weaknesses: it struggles with varying density and it is sensitive to $\epsilon$ in high dimensions. See curse of dimensionality.

heading: Hierarchical and spectral clustering
text:
Agglomerative clustering starts with one cluster per point and merges the closest pair. The linkage rule sets the meaning of closest.

| Linkage | Distance between clusters |
|---|---|
| Single | Minimum pairwise distance |
| Complete | Maximum pairwise distance |
| Average | Mean pairwise distance |
| Ward | Increase in within cluster variance |

Spectral clustering builds a similarity graph, computes the graph Laplacian, takes the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues, and runs k-means in that embedding. It handles non-convex shapes because it clusters in a space where the shape becomes simple. See eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

heading: Choosing K
text:
- Elbow method. Plot $J$ against $K$ and look for a bend.
- Silhouette score. For point $i$ with mean intra-cluster distance $a_i$ and mean nearest-cluster distance $b_i$,

$$
s_i = \frac{b_i - a_i}{\max(a_i, b_i)} \in [-1, 1].
$$

- Gap statistic. Compare $\log J$ against a uniform reference.
- BIC or AIC for a GMM, because a GMM has a likelihood.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


def kmeans(X, k, iters=100, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    centers = X[rng.choice(len(X), size=k, replace=False)]
    for _ in range(iters):
        d = ((X[:, None, :] - centers[None, :, :]) ** 2).sum(-1)
        labels = d.argmin(1)
        new = np.stack([
            X[labels == j].mean(0) if np.any(labels == j) else centers[j]
            for j in range(k)
        ])
        if np.allclose(new, centers):
            break
        centers = new
    inertia = ((X - centers[labels]) ** 2).sum()
    return labels, centers, inertia

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = np.vstack([rng.normal(0, 1, (100, 2)), rng.normal(5, 1, (100, 2))])
labels, centers, inertia = kmeans(X, 2)
print(centers, round(float(inertia), 2))
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not run k-means without scaling features to comparable ranges.

Do not use the inertia value to compare different values of $K$ directly. Inertia always falls as $K$ grows.

Do not treat cluster ids as class labels. They carry no order or meaning.

heading: Overview
text: A convolution slides a small learned kernel over the input and shares its weights across all positions. This gives translation equivariance, local connectivity, and a parameter count that does not depend on the input size.

heading: The convolution operation
text:
For a 2D input $x$ and kernel $w$ of size $k \times k$, the output at position $(i,j)$ for output channel $o$ is

$$
y_{o,i,j}
=
b_o + \sum_{c=1}^{C_{\text{in}}}\sum_{u=0}^{k-1}\sum_{v=0}^{k-1}
w_{o,c,u,v}\, x_{c,\, i+u,\, j+v}.
$$

Deep learning libraries implement cross correlation, not true convolution. True convolution flips the kernel. The difference does not matter because the kernel is learned.

heading: Three properties
text:
1. **Local connectivity.** Each output depends on a small input patch. This encodes the prior that nearby pixels are related.
2. **Weight sharing.** The same kernel applies at every position. A feature detector learned in one place works everywhere.
3. **Translation equivariance.** Shifting the input shifts the output by the same amount:

$$
\text{conv}(\text{shift}(x)) = \text{shift}(\text{conv}(x)).
$$

Pooling and a global average add approximate translation invariance on top of equivariance.

heading: Output size
text:
For input size $H$, kernel $k$, padding $p$, stride $s$, and dilation $d$:

$$
H_{\text{out}}
=
\left\lfloor \frac{H + 2p - d(k-1) - 1}{s}\right\rfloor + 1 .
$$

With $d=1$ this reduces to

$$
H_{\text{out}} = \left\lfloor\frac{H + 2p - k}{s}\right\rfloor + 1 .
$$

"Same" padding with $s=1$ uses $p = (k-1)/2$ for odd $k$.

heading: Parameter and compute count
text:
A conv layer with $C_{\text{in}}$ input channels, $C_{\text{out}}$ output channels, and a $k\times k$ kernel has

$$
\text{params} = C_{\text{out}}\big(C_{\text{in}}k^2 + 1\big).
$$

The count does not depend on the spatial size. A dense layer on a $224\times224\times3$ image with 1000 outputs needs about $1.5\times 10^8$ weights. A $3\times3$ conv with 64 channels needs about 1792.

The multiply-accumulate count is

$$
\text{MACs} = H_{\text{out}}\, W_{\text{out}}\, C_{\text{out}}\, C_{\text{in}}\, k^2 .
$$

heading: Receptive field
text:
The receptive field is the input region that affects one output unit.

For a stack of layers with kernel sizes $k_\ell$ and strides $s_\ell$, the receptive field grows as

$$
r_L = r_{L-1} + (k_L - 1)\prod_{\ell=1}^{L-1}s_\ell .
$$


Let $r_\ell$ be the receptive field of one unit at layer $\ell$, measured in input pixels. Let $j_\ell$ be the jump, which is the input distance between two neighboring units at layer $\ell$.

The jump multiplies by the stride at each layer:

$$
j_\ell = j_{\ell-1} s_\ell ,
\qquad j_0 = 1 .
$$

One unit at layer $\ell$ reads $k_\ell$ neighboring units of layer $\ell-1$. Those units span

$$
r_{\ell-1} + (k_\ell - 1) j_{\ell-1}
$$

input pixels, because each extra unit adds one jump of coverage.

Therefore

$$
r_\ell = r_{\ell-1} + (k_\ell-1)j_{\ell-1},
\qquad
j_{\ell-1} = \prod_{m=1}^{\ell-1}s_m .
$$


Two stacked $3\times3$ convs give a $5\times5$ receptive field with fewer parameters than one $5\times5$ conv, and they add a nonlinearity. This is the VGG design rule.

Dilation increases the receptive field without extra parameters. A dilated conv with rate $d$ acts like a kernel of effective size $d(k-1)+1$.

heading: Common layer types
text:
| Layer | Purpose |
|---|---|
| $3\times3$ conv | Standard feature extractor |
| $1\times1$ conv | Mixes channels, changes channel count, cheap |
| Depthwise conv | One filter per input channel |
| Depthwise separable | Depthwise then $1\times1$, about $1/k^2$ of the cost |
| Max pool | Downsample, small translation invariance |
| Average pool | Downsample, smoother |
| Global average pool | Replaces the flatten and dense head |
| Transposed conv | Upsamples for segmentation and generation |

Depthwise separable convolution reduces cost from $C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}k^2$ to $C_{\text{in}}k^2 + C_{\text{in}}C_{\text{out}}$ per position.

heading: Architectural patterns
text:
- **LeNet and AlexNet.** Conv, pool, then dense.
- **VGG.** Only $3\times3$ convs, stacked deep.
- **ResNet.** Residual connections $y = x + F(x)$ let gradients flow directly and allow very deep stacks. See exploding and vanishing gradients.
- **Inception.** Parallel branches with different kernel sizes.
- **U-Net.** Encoder plus decoder with skip connections for segmentation.
- **ConvNeXt.** Modern conv design tuned with transformer style choices.

Batch normalization after the conv and before the activation is a standard block.

heading: Backward pass
text:
The gradient with respect to the input of a convolution is a convolution of the output gradient with the flipped kernel. This is a full correlation, sometimes called a transposed convolution.

The gradient with respect to the kernel is a correlation between the input and the output gradient:

$$
\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{o,c,u,v}}
=
\sum_{i,j}\frac{\partial L}{\partial y_{o,i,j}}\, x_{c,i+u,j+v}.
$$

Weight sharing means every position contributes to the same gradient. That sum is the reason CNNs are data efficient.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


def conv2d_naive(x, w, b, stride=1, pad=0):
    """x: (C_in, H, W), w: (C_out, C_in, k, k), b: (C_out,)"""
    C_in, H, W = x.shape
    C_out, _, k, _ = w.shape
    xp = np.pad(x, ((0, 0), (pad, pad), (pad, pad)))
    H_out = (H + 2 * pad - k) // stride + 1
    W_out = (W + 2 * pad - k) // stride + 1
    out = np.zeros((C_out, H_out, W_out))
    for o in range(C_out):
        for i in range(H_out):
            for j in range(W_out):
                patch = xp[:, i * stride:i * stride + k, j * stride:j * stride + k]
                out[o, i, j] = np.sum(patch * w[o]) + b[o]
    return out

x = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=(3, 8, 8))
w = np.random.default_rng(1).normal(size=(4, 3, 3, 3)) * 0.1
b = np.zeros(4)
print(conv2d_naive(x, w, b, stride=1, pad=1).shape)
```

Real implementations use im2col plus a matrix multiply, or a direct kernel such as Winograd or FFT convolution.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not confuse equivariance with invariance. Convolution is equivariant. Pooling adds partial invariance.

Do not forget that the parameter count is independent of the input resolution, while the compute cost is not.

Do not use a large dense head after the last conv when a global average pool works. The dense head holds most of the parameters.

Do not set padding by guessing. Use the output size formula.

heading: Overview
text: A confidence interval is a range made by a procedure with a stated long-run coverage rate. It does not assign probability to a fixed parameter.

heading: Core idea
text:
A confidence interval estimates an unknown population parameter.

A common form is:

$$
\text{estimate} \pm \text{critical value} \times \text{standard error}.
$$

The standard error measures the sampling variation of the estimate.

For a sample mean with known standard deviation $\sigma$:

$$
\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

heading: Meaning of 95 percent confidence
text:
A 95 percent confidence interval comes from a procedure.

If you repeat the full sampling procedure many times, about 95 percent of the intervals contain the true parameter.

The parameter is fixed in the frequentist view.

The interval is random because it depends on the sample.

heading: Unknown variance
text:
Usually, the population standard deviation is unknown.

Then use the sample standard deviation $s$ and a $t$ critical value:

$$
\bar{x} \pm t_{\alpha/2,n-1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

The $t$ distribution has heavier tails than the normal distribution.

This accounts for uncertainty from estimating the variance.

heading: Standard error
text:
For independent samples with variance $\sigma^2$, the sample mean has variance:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar{X})
=
\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

Thus, the standard error is:

$$
\operatorname{SE}(\bar{X})
=
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Let:

$$
\bar{X}
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i.
$$

Assume the $X_i$ are independent and each has variance $\sigma^2$.

Then:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar{X})
=
\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\right).
$$

Pull out the constant:

$$
=
\frac{1}{n^2}\operatorname{Var}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_i\right).
$$

Independence lets variances add:

$$
=
\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Var}(X_i).
$$

Substitute $\sigma^2$:

$$
=
\frac{1}{n^2}n\sigma^2
=
\frac{\sigma^2}{n}.
$$

heading: Bootstrap intervals
text:
A bootstrap interval estimates uncertainty by resampling the observed data.

A simple percentile bootstrap works as follows.

1. Sample $n$ points with replacement from the data.

2. Compute the statistic.

3. Repeat many times.

4. Use quantiles of the bootstrap statistics.

Bootstrap methods help when analytic standard errors are hard.

heading: Code example
text:
```python

from scipy import stats

x = np.array([1.2, 0.9, 1.4, 1.1, 1.0])
n = len(x)

mean = np.mean(x)
se = stats.sem(x)
crit = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=n - 1)

lo = mean - crit * se
hi = mean + crit * se

print(lo, hi)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not say there is a 95 percent probability that this fixed interval contains the fixed parameter.

Do not ignore dependence between samples.

Do not confuse confidence intervals with prediction intervals.

heading: Overview
text: A convex function lies below the line segment between any two points. Any local minimum is also global.

heading: Core idea
text:
A function $f$ is convex if:

$$
f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)
\le
\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y),
$$

for all $x,y$ and $\lambda \in [0,1]$.

This means the graph bends upward.

heading: First-order condition
text:
For differentiable convex $f$:

$$
f(y) \ge f(x)+\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x).
$$

The tangent plane is a global lower bound.

heading: Second-order condition
text:
For twice differentiable $f$, convexity is equivalent to:

$$
\nabla^2 f(x) \succeq 0
$$

for all $x$ in the domain.

See Hessian and Positive Semi-Definite.

heading: Local and global minima
text:
Every local minimum of a convex function is global.


Let $x^\star$ be a local minimum.

Assume there is a point $y$ with:

$$
f(y) < f(x^\star).
$$

For $\lambda \in (0,1)$, define:

$$
z_\lambda = (1-\lambda)x^\star+\lambda y.
$$

Convexity gives:

$$
f(z_\lambda)
\le
(1-\lambda)f(x^\star)+\lambda f(y).
$$

Since $f(y)<f(x^\star)$:

$$
f(z_\lambda)<f(x^\star).
$$

For small $\lambda$, $z_\lambda$ is near $x^\star$.

This contradicts that $x^\star$ is a local minimum.

Therefore no such $y$ exists.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not assume every optimization problem is convex.

Do not confuse convex functions with convex sets.

Do not assume strict convexity when only convexity is given.

heading: Overview
text: Cross-validation splits data into folds. Each fold serves as validation once, and the scores are averaged.

heading: Core idea
text:
Cross-validation estimates performance on unseen data.

In $k$-fold cross-validation, split data into $k$ folds.

For each fold:

1. Train on the other folds.
2. Validate on the held-out fold.
3. Store the score.

Then average the scores.

heading: Why use it
text:
A single train-validation split can be noisy.

Cross-validation uses more of the data for both training and validation.

It is useful when data is limited.

heading: Stratification
text:
For classification, stratified folds preserve class proportions.

This reduces fold-to-fold variation for imbalanced classes.

heading: Nested cross-validation
text:
Nested cross-validation separates model selection from performance estimation.

The inner loop selects hyperparameters.

The outer loop estimates generalization.

This reduces selection bias.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring="accuracy")
mean_score = scores.mean()
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not preprocess the full dataset before splitting.

Do not tune hyperparameters on the outer validation fold.

Do not use random folds for time-series data.

heading: Overview
text: Volume grows exponentially with dimension, so any fixed sample covers less of the space. Distances between random points also become almost equal, which weakens methods that rely on nearest neighbors.

heading: Core idea
text:
Let the data live in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Three effects appear as $d$ grows.

1. Sample sparsity. The number of points needed to cover the space grows exponentially in $d$.
2. Volume concentration. Almost all volume of a ball sits near its surface.
3. Distance concentration. The ratio of the farthest to the nearest distance goes to one.

heading: Sample sparsity
text:
Split each axis of the unit cube into $m$ bins. The cube then has $m^d$ cells.

To keep one point per cell you need $n = m^d$ points.

For $m=10$ and $d=10$ you need $10^{10}$ points.

A local method such as k-nearest neighbours needs neighbors that are truly close. In high dimensions such neighbors do not exist for a normal sample size.

heading: Volume near the surface
text:
Take the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$. Compare it with the inner ball of radius $1-\epsilon$.

The fraction of volume in the outer shell is

$$
1 - (1-\epsilon)^d .
$$

For $\epsilon = 0.01$ and $d = 500$ this fraction is about $0.993$.

The volume of a ball of radius $r$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ is

$$
V_d(r) = C_d r^d ,
$$

where $C_d$ depends only on the dimension.

The inner ball has volume

$$
V_d(1-\epsilon) = C_d (1-\epsilon)^d .
$$

The ratio of inner volume to total volume is

$$
\frac{C_d(1-\epsilon)^d}{C_d 1^d} = (1-\epsilon)^d .
$$

So the shell holds the remaining fraction

$$
1 - (1-\epsilon)^d .
$$

Because $0 < 1-\epsilon < 1$, the term $(1-\epsilon)^d$ goes to zero as $d$ grows. The shell fraction goes to one.

heading: Distance concentration
text:
Draw $n$ independent points from a fixed distribution with independent coordinates. Let $D_{\min}$ and $D_{\max}$ be the smallest and largest distance from a query point.

Under mild conditions,

$$
\frac{D_{\max} - D_{\min}}{D_{\min}} \to 0
\quad \text{as } d \to \infty .
$$

The reason is simple. A squared Euclidean distance is a sum of $d$ per-axis terms. The mean of that sum grows like $d$. The standard deviation grows like $\sqrt{d}$. So the relative spread shrinks like $1/\sqrt{d}$.

Nearest neighbor search then loses meaning, because every point is about equally far away.

heading: Effect on models
text:
High dimension raises variance for flexible models. See bias-variance tradeoff.

Distance based methods degrade first. Linear models with strong regularisation degrade last.

Kernel bandwidth selection also becomes hard, because a bandwidth that holds enough points is no longer local.

heading: Why real data still works
text:
Real data often lies near a low dimensional manifold inside the high dimensional space. This is the manifold hypothesis.

The effective dimension is then much smaller than $d$.

Useful responses to high dimension include:

- feature selection and dimensionality reduction,
- structural priors such as convolution in CNNs,
- strong regularization,
- more data along the directions that matter.

heading: Code example
text:
```python

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

for d in [2, 10, 100, 1000]:
    x = rng.normal(size=(1000, d))
    q = rng.normal(size=(1, d))
    dist = np.linalg.norm(x - q, axis=1)
    ratio = (dist.max() - dist.min()) / dist.min()
    print(d, round(float(ratio), 3))
```

The printed ratio shrinks as the dimension grows.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not assume that adding features always helps. Extra noisy features raise variance.

Do not trust Euclidean distance in very high dimension without a check.

Do not confuse ambient dimension with intrinsic dimension.

heading: Overview
text: Whitening applies a linear map $W$ so that the transformed data has identity covariance. PCA whitening rotates into the eigenbasis and rescales. ZCA whitening rotates back, which keeps the data visually close to the original.

heading: Goal
text:
Let $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with mean $\mu$ and covariance $\Sigma$. Whitening finds $W$ such that

$$
z = W(x-\mu),
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(z) = I .
$$

The result has unit variance in every direction and zero correlation between features.

heading: The eigendecomposition solution
text:
Write the eigendecomposition

$$
\Sigma = U\Lambda U^\top ,
$$

where $U$ is orthogonal and $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d)$ with $\lambda_j > 0$.

PCA whitening uses

$$
W_{\mathrm{PCA}} = \Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top .
$$

ZCA whitening uses

$$
W_{\mathrm{ZCA}} = U\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top = \Sigma^{-1/2}.
$$

Let $z = W(x-\mu)$ with $W = \Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top$.

The covariance of a linear map is

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(z) = W\Sigma W^\top .
$$

Substitute $\Sigma = U\Lambda U^\top$:

$$
\operatorname{Cov}(z)
=
\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top\, U\Lambda U^\top\, U\Lambda^{-1/2}.
$$

Since $U$ is orthogonal, $U^\top U = I$:

$$
=
\Lambda^{-1/2}\Lambda\Lambda^{-1/2}
=
\Lambda^{-1/2}\Lambda^{1/2}\Lambda^{1/2}\Lambda^{-1/2}
=
I .
$$

The same computation with $W_{\mathrm{ZCA}} = U\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top$ gives

$$
U\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top U\Lambda U^\top U\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top
=
U\Lambda^{-1/2}\Lambda\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top
=
UU^\top
=
I .
$$

heading: Whitening is not unique
text:
If $W$ whitens, then so does $RW$ for any orthogonal $R$, because

$$
(RW)\Sigma(RW)^\top = R I R^\top = I .
$$

So the whitening transform is defined only up to a rotation.

| Choice | Formula | Property |
|---|---|---|
| PCA | $\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top$ | Axes align with principal components |
| ZCA | $U\Lambda^{-1/2}U^\top$ | Closest to the identity in Frobenius norm |
| Cholesky | $L^{-1}$ with $\Sigma = LL^\top$ | Triangular, cheap |

ZCA is the standard choice for image data because it preserves spatial structure and looks like local edge enhancement.

heading: Numerical stability
text:
Small eigenvalues make $\lambda^{-1/2}$ huge and amplify noise.

Two standard fixes exist.

1. Add a regularizer:

$$
W = (\Sigma + \epsilon I)^{-1/2}.
$$

2. Drop directions with tiny eigenvalues. This is whitening plus dimensionality reduction.

Always fit $\mu$, $U$, and $\Lambda$ on the training set only. Applying the same transform to validation and test data prevents leakage.

heading: Why whitening helps optimization
text:
For a linear model with squared loss, the Hessian is proportional to the input covariance:

$$
H = \frac{2}{n} X^\top X .
$$

Whitening makes $X^\top X \propto I$, so the condition number becomes one. Gradient descent then converges in a single well scaled step direction.

This is the same motivation behind batch normalization, which whitens per feature within a mini-batch but skips the expensive decorrelation across features.

heading: Standardization compared with whitening
text:
| Operation | Effect on covariance |
|---|---|
| Centering | Mean becomes zero, covariance unchanged |
| Standardization | Diagonal becomes one, off-diagonal correlations remain |
| Whitening | Full covariance becomes the identity |

Standardization costs $O(d)$. Whitening costs $O(d^3)$ for the decomposition, so it is impractical for very large $d$.

heading: Code example
text:
```python

def fit_whitening(X, eps=1e-5, mode="zca"):
    mu = X.mean(axis=0)
    Xc = X - mu
    cov = (Xc.T @ Xc) / (len(X) - 1)
    lam, U = np.linalg.eigh(cov)
    inv_sqrt = np.diag(1.0 / np.sqrt(lam + eps))
    W = inv_sqrt @ U.T
    if mode == "zca":
        W = U @ W
    return mu, W

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = rng.normal(size=(3, 3))
X = rng.normal(size=(2000, 3)) @ A.T

mu, W = fit_whitening(X)
Z = (X - mu) @ W.T
print(np.round(np.cov(Z, rowvar=False), 3))
```

The printed covariance should be close to the identity.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not fit the whitening matrix on the full dataset including the test split.

Do not omit the epsilon term. Near zero eigenvalues will explode.

Do not confuse standardization with whitening. Standardization leaves correlations in place.

heading: Overview
text: A decision tree picks the split that most reduces an impurity measure, then recurses. Trees are readable and need no feature scaling, but a single deep tree overfits. Pruning and ensembles fix that.

heading: Structure
text:
A tree is a set of internal nodes and leaves.

- An internal node holds a test such as $x_j \le t$.
- Each leaf holds a prediction. Classification uses the majority class or the class frequencies. Regression uses the mean target.

Prediction walks from the root to a leaf. The cost is $O(\text{depth})$.

The model is piecewise constant on axis aligned boxes.

heading: Impurity measures
text:
For classification with class proportions $p_1,\dots,p_K$ in a node:

$$
\text{Gini} = 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k^2 ,
$$

$$
\text{Entropy} = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k \log_2 p_k .
$$

For regression:

$$
\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{i\in S}(y_i - \bar{y}_S)^2 .
$$

Both Gini and entropy peak at a uniform distribution and reach zero at a pure node. See entropy.

Gini is slightly cheaper because it needs no logarithm. The two rarely produce different trees.

heading: Choosing a split
text:
The impurity decrease of a split of node $S$ into $S_L$ and $S_R$ is

$$
\Delta
=
I(S)
-\frac{|S_L|}{|S|}I(S_L)
-\frac{|S_R|}{|S|}I(S_R).
$$

CART evaluates every feature and every candidate threshold, then takes the largest $\Delta$.

For a numeric feature, sort the values and test midpoints between consecutive distinct values. Sorting once per feature makes the search cost $O(nd\log n)$ at the root.


Let $I$ be a concave function of the class proportion vector. Both Gini and entropy are concave.

Let $\lambda = |S_L|/|S|$, so the right child has weight $1-\lambda$. The parent proportions are the weighted average of the child proportions:

$$
p_S = \lambda p_{S_L} + (1-\lambda) p_{S_R}.
$$

Concavity gives

$$
I(p_S)
=
I\big(\lambda p_{S_L} + (1-\lambda)p_{S_R}\big)
\ge
\lambda I(p_{S_L}) + (1-\lambda) I(p_{S_R}).
$$

Therefore

$$
\Delta = I(p_S) - \lambda I(p_{S_L}) - (1-\lambda)I(p_{S_R}) \ge 0 .
$$

A split never increases weighted impurity. Equality holds when both children have the same class distribution as the parent.


Because $\Delta \ge 0$ always, a greedy tree can grow until every leaf is pure. That is why you must limit growth.

heading: Overfitting control
text:
| Control | Effect |
|---|---|
| `max_depth` | Caps the number of splits on a path |
| `min_samples_split` | Blocks splits on small nodes |
| `min_samples_leaf` | Forces leaves to hold enough data |
| `max_features` | Limits features considered per split |
| `min_impurity_decrease` | Requires a useful gain |
| Cost-complexity pruning | Removes weak subtrees after growth |

Cost-complexity pruning minimizes

$$
R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha |T| ,
$$

where $R(T)$ is the training error and $|T|$ is the number of leaves. Increasing $\alpha$ produces a nested sequence of subtrees. Pick $\alpha$ with cross validation.

heading: Strengths and weaknesses
text:
Strengths:

- No feature scaling is needed. Splits use order only.
- The model handles mixed numeric and categorical features.
- The rules are readable.
