heading: Causal masking
text:
For autoregressive models, a token cannot attend to future tokens.

FlashAttention applies the causal mask inside each tile.

It still computes exact masked attention.

It only changes the order of computation.

heading: Code example
text:
This code shows naive attention.

FlashAttention returns the same output, but it avoids the full score matrix.

```python



def attention(q, k, v, causal=False):
    d_k = q.shape[-1]
    scores = q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / d_k**0.5

    if causal:
        t = q.shape[-2]
        mask = torch.triu(torch.ones(t, t, device=q.device), diagonal=1).bool()
        scores = scores.masked_fill(mask, float("-inf"))

    weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
    return weights @ v
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not call FlashAttention an approximation.

Do not say it removes the quadratic compute cost.

It keeps the $O(n^2)$ attention pattern.

It mainly reduces memory traffic and stored activations.

heading: Overview
text: Griffin uses recurrent gated blocks and local attention. It aims to keep long-context memory with lower inference cost than full attention.

heading: Core idea
text:
Griffin is a hybrid architecture for sequence modeling.

It combines local attention with recurrent gated layers.

The recurrent layers carry state across tokens.

The local attention layers model nearby token interactions.

This design can reduce the cost of long-context inference.

heading: Recurrent gated state
text:
A simple gated recurrence has the form:

$$
h_t = a_t \odot h_{t-1} + (1-a_t)\odot \tilde{x}_t.
$$

The gate $a_t$ controls how much old state remains.

A value near one keeps memory.

A value near zero replaces memory with new input.

Griffin uses richer gated recurrent blocks than this simple form.

The idea is still state update through time.

heading: Local attention
text:
Local attention restricts each token to a nearby window.

This avoids full quadratic attention over all past tokens.

The recurrent state gives another path for long-range information.

Use causal attention for the mask idea.

heading: Comparison to Transformers
text:
A full Transformer attends to many earlier tokens directly.

Griffin compresses part of the history into recurrent state.

This can make decoding cheaper.

It can also change the failure modes.

A small state can forget details that full attention could retrieve.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not call Griffin a plain RNN.

Do not call it a standard Transformer.

Do not assume recurrent state stores all past tokens exactly.

Do not ignore the role of local attention.

heading: Overview
text: Scaled dot-product attention divides logits by $\sqrt{d_k}$. This keeps logit variance controlled and helps prevent softmax saturation.

heading: Core idea
text:
Attention uses dot products between queries and keys.

For a query $q$ and key $k$:

$$
s = q^\top k.
$$

Scaled attention uses:

$$
s = \frac{q^\top k}{\sqrt{d_k}}.
$$

Here $d_k$ is the key dimension.

The scale appears inside causal attention and cross attention.

heading: Why scale by square root
text:
Assume each component of $q$ and $k$ has mean zero and variance one.

Assume components are independent.

Then:

$$
q^\top k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i.
$$

Each product has variance one.

The sum has variance $d_k$.

Dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ gives variance near one.


Let:

$$
s = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} q_i k_i.
$$

Assume $q_i$ and $k_i$ are independent.

Assume each has mean zero and variance one.

Then:

$$
\mathbb{E}[q_i k_i]=0.
$$

Also:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(q_i k_i)
=
\mathbb{E}[q_i^2 k_i^2]
=
\mathbb{E}[q_i^2]\mathbb{E}[k_i^2]
=
1.
$$

The terms are independent, so variances add:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(s)=d_k.
$$

For $s/\sqrt{d_k}$:

$$
\operatorname{Var}\left(\frac{s}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)
=
\frac{d_k}{d_k}
=
1.
$$

heading: Softmax saturation
text:
Large logits make softmax very sharp.

A sharp softmax can produce small gradients for most positions.

The scaling factor keeps logits in a safer range.

It does not solve all stability problems.

heading: Code example
text:
```python



def scaled_attention_scores(q, k):
    d_k = q.shape[-1]
    return q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) / d_k**0.5

scores = scaled_attention_scores(q, k)
weights = F.softmax(scores, dim=-1)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not divide by $d_k$.

Do not apply the scale after softmax.

Do not confuse this with LLM scaling laws.

Use scaling laws for model-size scaling.

heading: Overview
text: Transformers use attention over tokens. RNNs update a hidden state step by step. S4 uses structured state-space dynamics for long sequences.

heading: Core comparison
text:
| Model family | Main history mechanism | Parallel training | Inference state |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Transformer LLM | attention over previous tokens | high | key-value cache |
| RNN | recurrent hidden state | limited | hidden state |
| S4 | structured state-space model | high with convolution | state or convolution cache |

Each family has different cost and memory behavior.

heading: Transformer LLMs
text:
A decoder-only LLM uses causal self-attention.

Each token can directly attend to previous tokens in context.

This gives strong retrieval inside the context window.

The cost is quadratic in sequence length during full attention training.

See causal attention.

heading: RNNs
text:
An RNN updates hidden state with:

$$
h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t).
$$

The state carries past information.

Training is less parallel than attention because steps depend on earlier steps.

RNNs can struggle with very long dependencies.

LSTMs and GRUs add gates to improve memory.

heading: S4
text:
S4 is a structured state-space sequence model.

It uses a linear dynamical system with special structure.

The model can compute long convolutions efficiently.

This gives long-range modeling with good parallelism.

See S4 for the detailed state-space view.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not say attention is always better.

Do not say RNNs cannot model long sequences.

Do not say S4 is just a Transformer.

The best choice depends on data, context length, hardware, and latency.

heading: Overview
text: LoRA freezes a base weight matrix and learns a low-rank update. It can reduce trainable parameters while keeping the original model usable.

heading: Core idea
text:
LoRA means low-rank adaptation.

For a frozen weight matrix $W$, LoRA learns:

$$
W' = W + \Delta W.
$$

The update has low rank:

$$
\Delta W = \frac{\alpha}{r}BA.
$$

Here $r$ is the rank.

If $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}}\times d_{\text{in}}}$, then:

$$
A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d_{\text{in}}}
$$

and:

$$
B \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\text{out}} \times r}.
$$

LoRA usually trains $A$ and $B$ only.

The base weight $W$ stays frozen.

heading: Why low rank helps
text:
A full update to $W$ has $d_{\text{out}}d_{\text{in}}$ parameters.

A LoRA update has:

$$
r(d_{\text{in}}+d_{\text{out}})
$$

parameters.

This can be much smaller when $r$ is small.

Use rank and span for the linear algebra.

heading: Where LoRA is applied
text:
LoRA often modifies attention projections.

Common targets are:

- query projection
- key projection
- value projection
- output projection
- feed-forward projection

The best target depends on the task and memory budget.

heading: Merge and unmerge
text:
After training, you can merge the update into the base weight:

$$
W_{\text{merged}} = W + \frac{\alpha}{r}BA.
$$

This removes extra LoRA operations at inference time.

You can also keep LoRA separate and swap adapters.

heading: Code example
Common mistakes
text:
Do not train the frozen base weight by accident.

Do not assume a larger rank always helps.

Do not forget to scale the low-rank update.

Do not merge adapters twice.

heading: Overview
text: A Mixture of Experts model has many expert networks, but a router activates only a few for each token. This increases parameter count without proportional compute.

heading: Core idea
text:
A dense feed-forward layer applies the same network to all tokens.

A Mixture of Experts layer has many expert networks.

A router scores experts for each token.

The model sends each token to the top $k$ experts.

The expert outputs are combined with router weights.

heading: Sparse activation
text:
If a layer has $E$ experts but uses only $k$ experts per token, then active compute depends on $k$.

Total parameter count depends on $E$.

This lets the model scale parameters faster than compute.

heading: Router
text:
For token representation $x$, the router can compute:

$$
p = \operatorname{softmax}(W_r x).
$$

Then it selects the top $k$ experts.

The output can be:

$$
y = \sum_{e \in \operatorname{TopK}(p)} p_e f_e(x).
$$

heading: Load balancing
text:
Routers can collapse to a few experts.

This wastes capacity.

MoE training often adds a load-balancing loss.

The loss encourages tokens to spread across experts.

heading: Common systems issues
text:
MoE creates communication between devices.

Tokens must move to the devices that hold their experts.

This can make routing and all-to-all communication expensive.

See communication primitives for the systems view.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not say all experts run for every token.

Do not ignore load balancing.

Do not compare active parameters and total parameters as the same value.

Do not assume MoE always improves latency.

heading: Overview
text: Perceiver maps large inputs into a fixed-size latent array with cross attention. It then processes the latent array with self-attention.

heading: Core idea
text:
Perceiver separates input size from internal attention cost.

It uses a learned latent array $Z$.

The latent array cross-attends to input features $X$.

Then the model applies self-attention inside the latent array.

If $X$ has $N$ items and $Z$ has $M$ latent items, then cross attention costs $O(NM)$.

Latent self-attention costs $O(M^2)$.

This helps when $M$ is much smaller than $N$.

heading: Cross attention bottleneck
text:
In Perceiver cross attention:

$$
Q = ZW_Q
$$

$$
K = XW_K
$$

$$
V = XW_V.
$$

The output updates the latent array.

See cross attention for the query, key, and value roles.

heading: Latent processing
text:
After cross attention, the model applies several latent self-attention blocks.

These blocks mix information inside the latent array.

The compute depends on $M$, not directly on $N$.

heading: Perceiver IO
text:
Perceiver IO adds flexible outputs.

Output queries attend to the latent array.

This lets the model produce labels, sequences, or dense predictions.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not say Perceiver removes attention.

It still uses attention.

Do not confuse input tokens with latent tokens.

Do not make $M$ too small for a hard task.

heading: Overview
text: Pretraining optimizes a self-supervised language-modeling loss on large data. It gives the model general capabilities before task-specific adaptation.

heading: Core idea
text:
Decoder-only LLMs usually train with next-token prediction.

Given tokens $x_1,\dots,x_T$, the model predicts each next token.

The objective is negative log likelihood:

$$
\mathcal{L}
=
-\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\log p_\theta(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\le t}).
$$

This is self-supervised.

The target token comes from the input text itself.

heading: Data mixture
text:
Pretraining data usually mixes many sources.

Examples include web text, books, code, and math data.

Data quality strongly affects the result.

Deduplication can reduce memorization.

Filtering can reduce harmful or low-quality text.

heading: Training loop
text:
A basic training step uses shifted inputs and labels.

```python


def lm_loss(model, token_ids):
    logits = model(token_ids[:, :-1])
    labels = token_ids[:, 1:]
    vocab = logits.shape[-1]
    return F.cross_entropy(logits.reshape(-1, vocab), labels.reshape(-1))
```

heading: Evaluation
text:
Perplexity is a common language-model metric.

It is the exponential of average negative log likelihood.

Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to the text.

Perplexity does not measure all useful behavior.

heading: Link to later adaptation
text:
Pretraining creates a base model.

Finetuning adapts it to tasks or formats.

RLHF can align outputs with preferences.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not train on validation data.

Do not ignore tokenizer changes.

Do not treat low perplexity as complete evaluation.

Do not forget data quality.

heading: Overview
text: Relative positional embeddings encode the offset between two tokens. They let attention depend on distance, not only absolute position.

heading: Core idea
text:
Absolute position embeddings attach a position to each token.

Relative positional embeddings attach a distance to each pair of tokens.

For positions $i$ and $j$, the relative offset is:

$$
r = i - j.
$$

The attention score can include a bias for this offset:

$$
s_{ij}
=
\frac{q_i^\top k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}
+
b_{i-j}.
$$

heading: Relative bias
text:
Many models use a learned relative bias table.

The table maps each offset or offset bucket to a scalar.

The scalar adds to the attention logit.

This is simple and efficient.

T5 uses relative position bias with buckets.

heading: Relative key embeddings
text:
Some methods use an embedding vector for each relative offset.

Then attention can include:

$$
q_i^\top a_{i-j}.
$$

This lets the query interact with relative position features.

Transformer-XL uses a more detailed relative attention form.

See Transformer-XL.

heading: ALiBi
text:
ALiBi adds a linear distance bias.

It penalizes far tokens by distance.

It does not require learned position embeddings.

It can help length extrapolation in some settings.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not confuse relative positions with absolute positions.

Do not forget that causal masks still apply.

Do not assume all relative methods use the same formula.

Do not ignore offset clipping or bucketing.

heading: Overview
text: RLHF uses preference labels to train a reward model. It then optimizes a language model to get high reward while staying near a reference model.

heading: Core idea
text:
RLHF means reinforcement learning from human feedback.

A common pipeline has three stages.

1. Train a base model with pretraining.

2. Supervised finetune it on good responses.

3. Optimize it with a reward model from human preferences.

The final stage often uses a KL penalty.

The penalty keeps the policy close to a reference model.

heading: Preference data
text:
Annotators compare two or more responses to the same prompt.

The data says which response is preferred.

This gives pairwise preference examples.

A reward model learns to score responses.

heading: Reward model loss
text:
For a preferred response $y_w$ and a rejected response $y_l$, a common loss is:

$$
\mathcal{L}
=
-\log \sigma(r_\phi(x,y_w)-r_\phi(x,y_l)).
$$

This trains the reward model to score the preferred response higher.

heading: Policy optimization
text:
The policy model generates responses.

The reward model scores them.

The training objective often includes:

$$
\mathbb{E}[r_\phi(x,y)]
-
\beta \operatorname{KL}(\pi_\theta(\cdot|x)\|\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot|x)).
$$

The KL term reduces reward hacking and distribution drift.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not treat the reward model as ground truth.

Do not optimize reward without checking generated samples.

Do not remove the KL penalty without a reason.

Do not confuse RLHF with supervised finetuning.

heading: Overview
text: RoPE applies position-dependent rotations to queries and keys. The resulting dot product depends on relative position.

heading: Core idea
text:
RoPE means rotary positional embedding.

It does not add a position vector to token embeddings.

Instead, it rotates query and key vectors by a position-dependent angle.

Attention then uses the rotated vectors.

This makes relative positions affect dot products.

heading: Two-dimensional rotation
text:
For a pair of features $(x_1,x_2)$ at position $m$, RoPE applies:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1' \\
x_2'
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(m\theta) & -\sin(m\theta) \\
\sin(m\theta) & \cos(m\theta)
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1 \\
x_2
\end{bmatrix}.
$$

The model applies this to pairs of channels with different frequencies.

heading: Relative position property
text:
Let $R_m$ be the rotation at position $m$.

For query $q$ at position $m$ and key $k$ at position $n$:

$$
(R_m q)^\top(R_n k)
=
q^\top R_{n-m}k.
$$

Thus the score depends on the relative offset $n-m$.


Rotation matrices satisfy:

$$
R_m^\top R_n = R_{n-m}.
$$

The attention dot product is:

$$
(R_m q)^\top(R_n k).
$$

Move the first rotation to the middle:

$$
q^\top R_m^\top R_n k.
$$

Substitute the rotation identity:

$$
q^\top R_{n-m} k.
$$

Thus the score depends on the relative offset.

heading: Context extension
text:
Many LLMs use RoPE.

Longer context can need RoPE scaling or interpolation.

These methods change the mapping from position to angle.

They try to reduce mismatch between training and inference lengths.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


def apply_rope_pair(x, cos, sin):
    x1 = x[..., 0::2]
    x2 = x[..., 1::2]
    y1 = x1 * cos - x2 * sin
    y2 = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return torch.stack((y1, y2), dim=-1).flatten(-2)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not add RoPE to values.

Most implementations rotate queries and keys.

Do not confuse RoPE with learned absolute positions.

Do not assume context extension works without validation.

heading: Overview
text: Scaling laws model how loss changes as data, parameters, and compute grow. They help choose model size and training tokens for a compute budget.

heading: Core idea
text:
LLM scaling laws are empirical relationships.

They often fit loss with power laws.

A common form is:

$$
L(N,D)
=
L_{\infty}
+
aN^{-\alpha}
+
bD^{-\beta}.
$$

Here $N$ is parameter count.

Here $D$ is the number of training tokens.

The constants come from experiments.

heading: Compute tradeoff
text:
Training compute grows roughly with parameters times tokens.

A simple estimate is:

$$
C \propto ND.
$$

For a fixed compute budget, you must choose $N$ and $D$.

A larger model trained on too few tokens can undertrain.

A smaller model trained on more tokens can perform better at the same compute.

heading: Compute-optimal training
text:
Compute-optimal scaling chooses model size and data size together.

Chinchilla-style results showed that many older LLMs used too many parameters for their token count.

The practical lesson is simple.

Use enough training tokens for the model size.

heading: What scaling laws do not guarantee
text:
Scaling laws extrapolate from measured runs.

They can fail after data quality changes.

They can fail after architecture changes.

They also do not predict all downstream skills.

Use them as planning tools, not proofs.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
def predicted_loss(n_params, n_tokens, l_inf, a, alpha, b, beta):
    return l_inf + a * n_params**(-alpha) + b * n_tokens**(-beta)

loss = predicted_loss(
    n_params=7e9,
    n_tokens=1.4e12,
    l_inf=1.5,
    a=100,
    alpha=0.08,
    b=200,
    beta=0.10,
)
print(loss)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not treat scaling laws as exact physical laws.

Do not ignore data quality.

Do not compare models with very different training recipes without care.

Do not optimize parameter count alone.

heading: Overview
text: Sinusoidal positional embeddings add fixed sine and cosine features to token embeddings. Different frequencies let the model infer positions and distances.

heading: Core idea
text:
A Transformer without position information treats tokens as a set.

Sinusoidal embeddings add position information.

For position $\text{pos}$ and channel index $i$:

$$
\operatorname{PE}(\text{pos},2i)
=
\sin\left(\frac{\text{pos}}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right)
$$

$$
\operatorname{PE}(\text{pos},2i+1)
=
\cos\left(\frac{\text{pos}}{10000^{2i/d_{\text{model}}}}\right).
$$

The model adds these features to token embeddings.

heading: Why use many frequencies
text:
Short wavelengths distinguish nearby positions.

Long wavelengths vary slowly across long ranges.

Together, they give position features at many scales.

The model can learn to combine these features.

heading: Fixed versus learned
text:
Sinusoidal embeddings are fixed.

They do not add learned parameters.

Learned absolute embeddings can fit training positions.

They can extrapolate poorly beyond the trained length.

Sinusoidal embeddings can define values at any position.

heading: Link to RoPE
text:
RoPE also uses sine and cosine.

But RoPE rotates queries and keys.

Sinusoidal embeddings add position vectors to token embeddings.

See RoPE for the rotation method.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


def sinusoidal_positions(length, dim):
    pos = torch.arange(length).float().unsqueeze(1)
    i = torch.arange(0, dim, 2).float()
    scale = 10000 ** (i / dim)
    pe = torch.zeros(length, dim)
    pe[:, 0::2] = torch.sin(pos / scale)
    pe[:, 1::2] = torch.cos(pos / scale)
    return pe
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not forget that even and odd channels use different functions.

Do not confuse fixed sinusoidal embeddings with learned position embeddings.

Do not assume position embeddings alone solve long-context limits.

heading: Overview
text: Tokenization converts text into token IDs. The tokenizer defines the model vocabulary and affects compression, unknown text, and generation behavior.

heading: Core idea
text:
LLMs operate on token IDs, not raw strings.

A tokenizer maps text to a sequence of IDs.

It also maps IDs back to text.

Common tokenizer families include:

- byte pair encoding
- WordPiece
- unigram language model tokenization
- byte-level tokenization

heading: Subword tokens
text:
A word can split into multiple subword tokens.

A common word can be one token.

A rare word can split into many tokens.

This keeps vocabulary size manageable.

It also lets the model represent new words.

heading: Byte pair encoding
text:
Byte pair encoding starts with small units.

It repeatedly merges frequent adjacent pairs.

After training, the merge list defines the tokenizer.

Encoding applies merges in the learned order.

heading: Vocabulary tradeoffs
text:
A larger vocabulary can reduce sequence length.

It also increases embedding and output projection size.

A smaller vocabulary can handle text more uniformly.

It can make sequences longer.

heading: Tokenization and generation
text:
Decoding produces token IDs.

The tokenizer converts these IDs back to text.

Some token boundaries can create surprising behavior.

For example, a leading space can be part of a token.

Use decoding techniques for sampling from token probabilities.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not assume tokens equal words.

Do not change the tokenizer without updating embeddings.

Do not compare token counts across different tokenizers without care.

Do not ignore byte fallback for unusual text.

heading: Overview
text: Transformer-XL extends Transformer context with cached hidden states from earlier segments. It also uses relative position information.

heading: Core idea
text:
A standard Transformer processes a fixed context window.

This can cause context fragmentation.

Transformer-XL splits a long sequence into segments.

For the current segment, it reuses hidden states from previous segments.

These cached states act as memory.

The model can attend beyond the current segment length.

heading: Segment recurrence
text:
Let $h_{\tau}^{n}$ be layer $n$ hidden states for segment $\tau$.

Transformer-XL builds the key and value memory from:

$$
\tilde{h}_{\tau}^{n-1}
=
[\operatorname{SG}(h_{\tau-1}^{n-1}); h_{\tau}^{n-1}].
$$

Here $\operatorname{SG}$ means stop-gradient.

The current segment can attend to old hidden states.

The old hidden states do not get gradients from the current segment.


Without stop-gradient, the current loss would backpropagate through all previous cached segments.

That would make the computation graph grow with sequence history.

Transformer-XL treats cached hidden states as constants.

Thus the current segment only stores gradients for the current computation.

This gives a longer effective context without full backpropagation through time.

heading: Relative positions
text:
Absolute positions do not transfer well across segments.

Transformer-XL uses relative position information.

This lets attention depend on distance between tokens.

See relative positional embeddings for common forms.

heading: Why it helps generation
text:
During generation, the model can cache prior states.

This lowers repeated computation.

It also gives tokens access to more history.

The idea relates to key-value caches in modern decoders.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not confuse segment recurrence with training an RNN.

Transformer-XL still uses attention inside each segment.

Do not backpropagate through an unlimited memory cache.

Do not use absolute positions alone across reused segments.

heading: Overview
text: Actor-critic methods use an actor to choose actions and a critic to estimate value. The critic supplies lower-variance learning signals for the actor.

heading: Core idea
text:
The actor is a policy:

$$
\pi_\theta(a \mid s).
$$

The critic estimates a value function.

Common critics estimate $V^\pi(s)$ or $Q^\pi(s,a)$.

The actor update uses a policy-gradient term:

$$
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\hat A_t.
$$

The critic helps compute $\hat A_t$.

heading: Critic training
text:
A value critic can minimize squared TD error:

$$
L_V
=
\left(
V_\phi(s_t)-
[r_t+\gamma V_\phi(s_{t+1})]
\right)^2.
$$

The critic does not need to be perfect.

It should give useful advantage estimates.

heading: Why use a critic
text:
Pure Monte Carlo policy gradients can have high variance.

A critic reduces variance through bootstrapping and baselines.

This can add bias if the critic is inaccurate.

See Variance Reduction in RL.

heading: Common variants
text:
A2C uses synchronous actor-critic updates.

A3C uses asynchronous workers.

PPO commonly uses an actor-critic architecture.

SAC uses actor-critic with entropy regularization.

See Soft Actor-Critic.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not train the actor through the critic target by accident.

Do not ignore critic loss scale.

Do not assume a lower critic loss always gives a better policy.

heading: Overview
text: AlphaGo combines neural networks with search. Policy networks guide candidate moves, value networks evaluate positions, and self-play improves the system.

heading: Core idea
text:
AlphaGo solved Go by combining learning and planning.

It used policy networks to propose strong moves.

It used value networks to estimate position strength.

It used Monte Carlo tree search to plan ahead.

heading: Training stages
text:
Early AlphaGo versions used supervised learning from human games.

They trained a policy network to imitate expert moves.

Then self-play reinforcement learning improved the policy.

A value network learned to predict game outcomes from positions.

heading: Monte Carlo tree search
text:
MCTS searches possible move sequences.

The policy network narrows the search to promising moves.

The value network evaluates leaf positions.

Search returns an improved move distribution.

heading: AlphaGo Zero
text:
AlphaGo Zero removed human game data.

It learned from self-play only.

It used the game rules and MCTS to create training targets.

This showed the strength of self-play with search.

heading: Link to MuZero
text:
MuZero extends this line.

It learns a latent dynamics model instead of using known game dynamics.

See MuZero.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not say AlphaGo is only a neural network.

Do not ignore MCTS.

Do not confuse AlphaGo with AlphaGo Zero.

heading: Overview
text: Bellman equations turn long-horizon return into a one-step recursion. They are the basis for value estimation, planning, and many reinforcement learning algorithms.

heading: Core idea
text:
The return satisfies:

$$
G_t = r_t + \gamma G_{t+1}.
$$

Taking conditional expectation gives a value recursion.

For a policy $\pi$:

$$
V^\pi(s)
=
\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi, s' \sim P}
\left[
R(s,a)+\gamma V^\pi(s')
\right].
$$

The action value function satisfies:

$$
Q^\pi(s,a)
=
\mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P}
\left[
R(s,a)+\gamma
\mathbb{E}_{a' \sim \pi(\cdot \mid s')}
Q^\pi(s',a')
\right].
$$

heading: Optimal Bellman equation
text:
The optimal value chooses the best action:

$$
V^*(s)
=
\max_a
\mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P}
\left[
R(s,a)+\gamma V^*(s')
\right].
$$

The optimal action value satisfies:

$$
Q^*(s,a)
=
\mathbb{E}_{s' \sim P}
\left[
R(s,a)+\gamma \max_{a'}Q^*(s',a')
\right].
$$

This equation appears in Q-Learning and TD Learning.

heading: Bellman backup
text:
A Bellman backup replaces a value estimate with a one-step target.

For Q-learning, the target is:

$$
y = r+\gamma \max_{a'}Q(s',a').
$$

For SARSA, the target uses the next sampled action.

See SARSA for the on-policy version.

heading: Proof idea
text:
Start with the discounted return:

$$
G_t=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k r_{t+k}.
$$

Split the first reward from the rest:

$$
G_t
=
r_t+
\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\gamma^k r_{t+k}.
$$

Factor out one $\gamma$:

$$
G_t
=
r_t+\gamma
\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\gamma^j r_{t+1+j}.
$$

The remaining sum is $G_{t+1}$.

Thus:

$$
G_t=r_t+\gamma G_{t+1}.
$$

Now condition on $s_t=s$ and take expectation under policy $\pi$.

This gives:

$$
V^\pi(s)
=
\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[r_t+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1}) \mid s_t=s].
$$

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not mix $V^\pi$ with $V^*$.

Do not use $\max$ in the policy evaluation equation.

Do not forget the expectation over transitions.

heading: Overview
text: Credit assignment asks how much responsibility each earlier action has for later outcomes. Delayed rewards make this problem hard.

heading: Core idea
text:
An action can affect rewards many steps later.

The credit assignment problem asks which actions caused the reward.

This is hard when rewards are delayed, sparse, or noisy.

A good algorithm gives useful learning signals to important decisions.

heading: Temporal credit
text:
Temporal credit assigns reward across time.

Monte Carlo returns assign the same future return to many past actions.

TD methods assign credit through bootstrapped value estimates.

Eligibility traces keep a decayed memory of visited states or actions.

GAE also mixes short and long credit paths.

See GAE.

heading: Structural credit
text:
Structural credit assigns reward across parts of a model or action.

For example, a multi-action policy may need to know which component mattered.

Neural networks use backpropagation for parameter credit.

RL adds the challenge that rewards can arrive after many decisions.

heading: Reward shaping
text:
Reward shaping gives intermediate rewards.

It can speed learning.

It can also change the task if designed incorrectly.

Potential-based shaping can preserve the optimal policy.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not reward only the final outcome when useful intermediate signals exist.

Do not add shaping rewards that change the desired behavior.

Do not confuse noisy rewards with delayed rewards.

heading: Overview
text: Curriculum learning changes the training task distribution over time. A good curriculum gives useful learning signals before the full task becomes feasible.

heading: Core idea
text:
A curriculum orders tasks or examples.

In reinforcement learning, the agent may start with easier environments.

Then training moves toward harder environments.

This can help when rewards are sparse or exploration is hard.

heading: Curriculum variables
text:
A curriculum can change many parts of a task.

It can change start states.

It can change goal distance.

It can change opponent strength.

It can change environment randomness.

It can change reward sparsity.

heading: Automatic curricula
text:
A hand-designed curriculum can work.

Automatic curricula choose tasks based on progress.

One common idea samples tasks where the agent improves fastest.

Another idea samples tasks near the agent's success boundary.

heading: Risks
text:
A curriculum can overfit the agent to easy tasks.

It can create a gap between training and final evaluation.

It can hide weaknesses if hard cases appear too late.

Domain randomization can help reduce this gap.

heading: Link to exploration
text:
Curricula help exploration by making reward easier to find early.

They also help credit assignment by shortening the path to success.

See Credit Assignment Problem.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not keep the curriculum too easy.

Do not change the final objective by accident.

Do not evaluate only on curriculum tasks.

heading: Overview
text: DPO uses preference pairs directly. It avoids an explicit reward model and a separate RL loop by optimizing a pairwise logistic objective.

heading: Core idea
text:
DPO trains on pairs $(x,y_w,y_l)$.

Here, $x$ is the prompt.

$y_w$ is the preferred response.

$y_l$ is the less preferred response.

DPO increases the relative log probability of $y_w$ over $y_l$.

It does this relative to a reference policy.

heading: Loss
text:
A common DPO loss is:

$$
L_{\mathrm{DPO}}
=
-\log \sigma
\left(
\beta
\left[
\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_w \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w \mid x)}
-
\log \frac{\pi_\theta(y_l \mid x)}{\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l \mid x)}
\right]
\right).
$$

The parameter $\beta$ controls the strength of the preference update.

The reference policy limits drift from the starting model.

heading: Connection to RL
text:
DPO comes from a KL-regularized RL objective.

The derivation maps rewards to log policy ratios.

This removes the need to train a separate reward model.

It also removes online rollout optimization in the basic method.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


chosen = logp_policy_w - logp_ref_w
rejected = logp_policy_l - logp_ref_l
logits = beta * (chosen - rejected)
loss = -F.logsigmoid(logits).mean()
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not train DPO on unordered samples.

Do not ignore the reference policy terms.

Do not treat DPO as value-based RL.

heading: Overview
text: Exploration tries uncertain actions to learn. Exploitation chooses actions that currently look best.

heading: Core idea
text:
A reinforcement learning agent must choose between two goals.

Exploration gathers new information.

Exploitation uses current estimates to get reward.

Too little exploration can trap the agent in a poor policy.

Too much exploration can waste reward.

heading: Epsilon-greedy
text:
An $\epsilon$-greedy policy chooses a random action with probability $\epsilon$.

It chooses the best known action otherwise.

For action values $Q(s,a)$:

$$
a =
\begin{cases}
\text{random action} & \text{with probability } \epsilon \\
\arg\max_a Q(s,a) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

This method is simple and common with Q-Learning and TD Learning.

heading: Other strategies
text:
Softmax exploration samples actions by value.

Entropy regularization rewards stochastic policies.

Upper confidence bound methods add optimism for uncertain actions.

Thompson sampling samples a model or value estimate from a posterior.

heading: Deep RL issues
text:
Sparse rewards make exploration hard.

Large state spaces make random exploration inefficient.

Intrinsic rewards can help agents seek novelty.

Demonstrations or curricula can also help.

See Curriculum Learning.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not evaluate a policy with exploration noise unless the metric requires it.

Do not keep $\epsilon$ too high after learning.

Do not assume random actions explore well in large spaces.

heading: Overview
text: GAE estimates advantages from a weighted sum of TD errors. The parameter $\lambda$ controls the bias-variance tradeoff.

heading: Core idea
text:
The one-step TD error is:

$$
\delta_t
=
r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t).
$$

Generalized Advantage Estimation defines:

$$
\hat A_t^{\mathrm{GAE}(\gamma,\lambda)}
=
\sum_{l=0}^{\infty}
(\gamma\lambda)^l \delta_{t+l}.
$$

In finite rollouts, the sum ends at the rollout boundary.

heading: Role of lambda
text:
When $\lambda=0$, GAE uses only one-step TD error.

This has lower variance and more bias.

When $\lambda=1$, GAE approaches a Monte Carlo-style estimate.

This has less bootstrap bias and more variance.

Thus, $\lambda$ controls a bias-variance tradeoff.

heading: Recursive computation
text:
GAE can be computed backward:

$$
\hat A_t
=
\delta_t+\gamma\lambda \hat A_{t+1}.
$$

This recursion makes implementation simple.

Use masks to stop the recursion at terminal states.

heading: Use with PPO
text:
PPO commonly uses GAE for advantage estimates.

The policy loss then weights log-probability ratios by $\hat A_t$.

See PPO.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
def compute_gae(rewards, values, dones, gamma, lam):
    adv = 0.0
    out = []
    for t in reversed(range(len(rewards))):
        mask = 1.0 - dones[t]
        delta = rewards[t] + gamma * values[t + 1] * mask - values[t]
        adv = delta + gamma * lam * mask * adv
        out.append(adv)
    return list(reversed(out))
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not forget terminal masks.

Do not use stale value estimates without care.

Do not assume larger $\lambda$ is always better.

heading: Overview
text: GRPO samples a group of outputs for the same prompt. It uses group-relative rewards as advantages, so it can avoid a separate value model.

heading: Core idea
text:
Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, is a policy optimization method for preference or reward-model training.

For each prompt, sample several responses from the policy.

Score each response with a reward model or rule.

Normalize rewards within the group.

Use the normalized reward as an advantage estimate.

heading: Group-relative advantage
text:
For rewards $r_1,\dots,r_G$ in one group:

$$
\hat A_i
=
\frac{r_i-\operatorname{mean}(r)}
{\operatorname{std}(r)+\epsilon}.
$$

This compares each response against other responses for the same prompt.

It removes the need for a learned value baseline in the basic setup.

heading: Objective
text:
GRPO commonly uses a clipped ratio objective like PPO.

It can also add a KL penalty against a reference policy.

A simplified objective uses:

$$
r_i(\theta)
=
\frac{\pi_\theta(y_i \mid x)}
{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_i \mid x)}.
$$

Then it weights the clipped ratio by $\hat A_i$.

heading: Why it can help
text:
Prompt difficulty can vary greatly.

Group normalization makes rewards more comparable within a prompt.

This can reduce variance from prompt-level reward scale.

See Variance Reduction in RL.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not normalize rewards across unrelated prompts without checking scale.

Do not omit the reference KL when policy drift matters.

Do not confuse GRPO with DPO, which uses a supervised preference loss.

heading: Overview
text: Importance sampling reweights samples from a behavior distribution to estimate an expectation under a target distribution. It enables off-policy evaluation but can add high variance.

heading: Core idea
text:
Suppose samples come from $q(x)$.

You want an expectation under $p(x)$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{p}[f(x)].
$$

Rewrite it as:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{p}[f(x)]
=
\mathbb{E}_{q}
\left[
\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}f(x)
\right].
$$

The ratio $p(x)/q(x)$ is the importance weight.

heading: Policy ratios
text:
In reinforcement learning, a trajectory has probability under a policy.

For a trajectory $\tau$:

$$
w(\tau)
=
\frac{p_{\pi}(\tau)}{p_{\mu}(\tau)}.
$$

If the dynamics match, the ratio reduces to policy probabilities:

$$
w(\tau)
=
\prod_t
\frac{\pi(a_t \mid s_t)}{\mu(a_t \mid s_t)}.
$$

Here, $\mu$ is the behavior policy.

The target policy is $\pi$.

heading: Variance problem
text:
Products of ratios can become very large or very small.

This can cause high variance.

Common fixes include clipping, per-decision weights, and normalized weights.

PPO also uses policy ratios with clipping.

See PPO.

heading: Proof
text:
Start with the target expectation:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{p}[f(x)]
=
\int f(x)p(x)\,dx.
$$

Multiply and divide by $q(x)$.

This requires $q(x)>0$ wherever $p(x)f(x)$ can be nonzero.

$$
\int f(x)p(x)\,dx
=
\int f(x)\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}q(x)\,dx.
$$

This is an expectation under $q$:

$$
=
\mathbb{E}_{q}
\left[
\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}f(x)
\right].
$$

heading: Code example
text:
```python


target_prob = np.array([0.8, 0.2])
behavior_prob = np.array([0.5, 0.5])
actions = np.array([0, 1, 0])
rewards = np.array([1.0, 0.0, 1.0])

weights = target_prob[actions] / behavior_prob[actions]
estimate = np.mean(weights * rewards)
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not use importance sampling when behavior probability is zero.

Do not ignore the variance of long products.

Do not clip weights without understanding the bias.

heading: Overview
text: A Markov decision process is the standard model for reinforcement learning. It defines states, actions, rewards, transitions, and the objective that an agent tries to maximize.

heading: Core idea
text:
A Markov decision process, or MDP, is a tuple:

$$
(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{A}, P, R, \gamma).
$$

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $\mathcal{S}$ | state space |
| $\mathcal{A}$ | action space |
| $P(s' \mid s,a)$ | transition distribution |
| $R(s,a)$ | reward function |
| $\gamma$ | discount factor |

At time $t$, the agent sees state $s_t$.

It chooses action $a_t$.

The environment returns reward $r_t$ and next state $s_{t+1}$.

The transition rule is:

$$
s_{t+1} \sim P(\cdot \mid s_t,a_t).
$$

heading: Return and objective
text:
The discounted return from time $t$ is:

$$
G_t
=
\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\gamma^k r_{t+k}.
$$

A policy $\pi(a \mid s)$ maps a state to an action distribution.

The goal is to find a policy with high expected return:

$$
J(\pi)
=
\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\left[G_0\right].
$$

Use Markov Property to understand why the current state can be sufficient.

heading: Value functions
text:
The state value function is:

$$
V^\pi(s)
=
\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G_t \mid s_t=s].
$$

The action value function is:

$$
Q^\pi(s,a)
=
\mathbb{E}_{\pi}[G_t \mid s_t=s,a_t=a].
$$

These functions are central to Bellman Equations.

heading: Code example
Common mistakes
text:
Do not confuse a state with an observation.

Do not assume rewards must be dense.

Do not use $\gamma=1$ in an infinite task without care.

heading: Overview
text: The Markov property says the future depends on the past only through the current state. This property lets value functions use $s_t$ instead of the full history.

heading: Core idea
text:
A process has the Markov property when:

$$
p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t,a_t,s_{t-1},a_{t-1},\dots)
=
p(s_{t+1} \mid s_t,a_t).
$$

The current state must contain all needed history.

If it does not, the problem is partially observable.

An observation can fail to be Markov.

A state can include memory, filtered estimates, or stacked frames.

heading: Why it matters
text:
The Markov property makes dynamic programming possible.

It gives recursive value equations.

For a policy $\pi$:

$$
V^\pi(s)
=
\mathbb{E}[r_t+\gamma V^\pi(s_{t+1}) \mid s_t=s].
$$

This recursion supports Bellman Equations.

heading: State versus observation
text:
The environment can have a hidden state.

The agent may see only an observation.

For example, one video frame may not show velocity.

Stacked frames can help recover velocity.

Recurrent policies can also store useful history.

heading: Practical test
text:
Ask whether two histories with the same state give the same next-state distribution.

If they do, the state is Markov.

If they do not, add more information to the state.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not assume each observation is Markov.

Do not ignore hidden variables.

Do not use a value function over a non-Markov state without care.

heading: Overview
text: Model-based methods use a model of environment dynamics for planning or imagined data. Model-free methods learn values or policies directly from experience.

heading: Core idea
text:
A model predicts environment behavior.

It can predict next states, rewards, or latent transitions.

Model-based RL uses this model for planning, control, or data generation.

Model-free RL does not explicitly learn transition dynamics for planning.

It learns a policy, a value function, or both.

heading: Model-based strengths
text:
Model-based methods can be data efficient.

They can plan before acting.

They can use simulated rollouts from learned models.

World models and MuZero are important examples.

See World Models and Dreamer and MuZero.

heading: Model-based risks
text:
A learned model can be wrong.

Planning can exploit model errors.

Long imagined rollouts can compound errors.

Short rollouts and uncertainty penalties can help.

heading: Model-free strengths
text:
Model-free methods can be simpler.

They avoid explicit dynamics modeling.

They can work well with enough data.

Q-learning, PPO, and SAC are common model-free methods.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not call any neural network a world model.

Do not assume model-based always means better performance.

Do not ignore model bias in imagined rollouts.

heading: Overview
text: Monte Carlo methods wait for observed returns. TD methods update earlier by using current value estimates in the target.

heading: Core idea
text:
Monte Carlo value estimation uses the sampled return:

$$
G_t=\sum_{k=0}^{T-t-1}\gamma^k r_{t+k}.
$$

A simple update is:

$$
V(s_t)
\leftarrow
V(s_t)+\alpha(G_t-V(s_t)).
$$

TD learning uses a one-step target:

$$
r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1}).
$$

The update is:

$$
V(s_t)
\leftarrow
V(s_t)+\alpha(r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)).
$$

heading: Bias and variance
text:
Monte Carlo targets are unbiased samples of the true return.

They can have high variance.

TD targets use estimated values.

They can have bias early in learning.

They often have lower variance.

This tradeoff also appears in GAE.

heading: Episode requirements
text:
Monte Carlo methods need complete episodes.

TD methods can learn in continuing tasks.

TD methods can update after each step.

heading: When to use each
text:
Use Monte Carlo when episodes are short and returns are easy to sample.

Use TD when rewards arrive slowly or tasks continue for a long time.

Many modern methods mix both views.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not say TD has no bias.

Do not say Monte Carlo always has lower error.

Do not use Monte Carlo returns before an episode ends.

heading: Overview
text: MuZero learns a latent model that predicts rewards, values, and policies. It uses Monte Carlo tree search over the latent model for planning.

heading: Core idea
text:
MuZero combines learning and planning.

It does not require known environment dynamics.

It does not need to reconstruct observations.

It learns a latent model useful for search.

heading: Model parts
text:
MuZero uses three learned functions.

The representation function maps an observation history to a latent state:

$$
h_0 = f_\theta(o_{\le t}).
$$

The dynamics function predicts the next latent state and reward:

$$
h_{k+1}, r_k = g_\theta(h_k,a_k).
$$

The prediction function outputs policy and value:

$$
p_k, v_k = p_\theta(h_k).
$$

heading: Planning
text:
MuZero runs Monte Carlo tree search in latent space.

The search uses predicted rewards, values, and policies.

The improved search policy becomes a training target.

The value target comes from real rewards and search estimates.

heading: Why it matters
text:
MuZero works without a hand-coded simulator.

It learns only what is needed for planning.

This separates it from models that reconstruct pixels.

See World Models and Dreamer.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not say MuZero learns a full observation simulator.

Do not say it is purely model-free.

Do not ignore the role of tree search.

heading: Overview
text: On-policy learning uses data from the policy being improved. Off-policy learning can use data from a different behavior policy.

heading: Core idea
text:
A behavior policy collects data.

A target policy is the policy being evaluated or improved.

In on-policy learning, the behavior policy and target policy are the same.

In off-policy learning, they can differ.

heading: Examples
text:
SARSA is on-policy in its basic form.

Q-learning is off-policy because it learns a greedy target while behavior can explore.

PPO is usually on-policy because it reuses recent data only within a small policy change.

See SARSA and Q-Learning and TD Learning.

heading: Why off-policy learning helps
text:
Off-policy learning can use replay buffers.

It can learn from old data.

It can learn from demonstrations.

It usually needs corrections when the data policy differs from the target policy.

Importance Sampling gives one correction method.

heading: Main tradeoffs
text:
On-policy methods are simple and stable.

They often use data less efficiently.

Off-policy methods can use data better.

They can suffer from distribution mismatch and unstable targets.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not call any replay-buffer method off-policy without checking the update.

Do not ignore how old data differs from current policy data.

Do not use importance weights without variance control.

heading: Overview
text: The policy gradient theorem turns return maximization into a gradient estimator. It uses the score function $\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)$ times a value signal.

heading: Core idea
text:
Let $\pi_\theta(a \mid s)$ be a differentiable policy.

The objective is expected return:

$$
J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim \pi_\theta}[G_0].
$$

A common policy gradient form is:

$$
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_{\pi_\theta}
\left[
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)
Q^{\pi_\theta}(s_t,a_t)
\right].
$$

The score term changes the policy probability.

The value term says whether the action was good.

heading: REINFORCE estimator
text:
A Monte Carlo estimator uses returns:

$$
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
\approx
\sum_t
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)G_t.
$$

This estimator is unbiased under standard assumptions.

It can have high variance.

Baselines reduce variance.

See Variance Reduction in RL.

heading: Baseline
text:
You can subtract a state-only baseline:

$$
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)
(Q(s_t,a_t)-b(s_t))
\right].
$$

The baseline does not change the expected gradient.

A common baseline is $V(s_t)$.

Then the weight becomes the advantage:

$$
A(s_t,a_t)=Q(s_t,a_t)-V(s_t).
$$

heading: Proof
text:
Write the objective over trajectories:

$$
J(\theta)
=
\int p_\theta(\tau)R(\tau)\,d\tau.
$$

Differentiate under the integral:

$$
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\int \nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau)R(\tau)\,d\tau.
$$

Use the identity:

$$
\nabla_\theta p_\theta(\tau)
=
p_\theta(\tau)\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau).
$$

Then:

$$
\nabla_\theta J(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}_{\tau}
[
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)R(\tau)
].
$$

The trajectory log probability contains policy terms and dynamics terms.

Dynamics do not depend on $\theta$.

Thus:

$$
\nabla_\theta \log p_\theta(\tau)
=
\sum_t \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t).
$$

This gives the REINFORCE estimator.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not differentiate through sampled actions directly for discrete actions.

Do not forget that baselines must not depend on the sampled action.

Do not ignore variance in long episodes.

heading: Overview
text: PPO is an on-policy actor-critic method. It uses clipped policy ratios so the new policy does not move too far from the data policy.

heading: Core idea
text:
PPO collects rollouts with an old policy.

It updates a new policy with probability ratio:

$$
r_t(\theta)
=
\frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}
{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}.
$$

The clipped surrogate objective is:

$$
L^{\mathrm{CLIP}}(\theta)
=
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\min
\left(
r_t(\theta)\hat A_t,
\operatorname{clip}(r_t(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat A_t
\right)
\right].
$$

heading: Why clipping helps
text:
Large policy updates can destroy performance.

The ratio measures how much action probability changes.

Clipping limits the objective incentive outside a trust region.

It is not a hard KL constraint.

Many implementations also monitor KL divergence.

heading: PPO training loop
text:
1. Collect rollouts with the current policy.

2. Estimate advantages, often with GAE.

3. Optimize the clipped policy loss for several epochs.

4. Train the value function.

5. Repeat with fresh rollouts.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


ratio = torch.exp(logp_new - logp_old)
unclipped = ratio * adv
clipped = torch.clamp(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps) * adv
policy_loss = -torch.mean(torch.minimum(unclipped, clipped))
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not reuse old rollouts for too many epochs.

Do not forget to detach old log probabilities.

Do not treat clipping as a full off-policy correction.

heading: Overview
text: Temporal-difference learning updates estimates before an episode ends. Q-learning is an off-policy TD method that learns the greedy optimal action value function.

heading: Core idea
text:
TD learning uses a bootstrapped target.

For value prediction:

$$
V(s_t)
\leftarrow
V(s_t)+\alpha
\left[
r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t)
\right].
$$

The term in brackets is the TD error:

$$
\delta_t
=
r_t+\gamma V(s_{t+1})-V(s_t).
$$

heading: Q-learning
text:
Q-learning estimates the optimal action value function.

Its update is:

$$
Q(s_t,a_t)
\leftarrow
Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha
\left[
r_t+\gamma \max_{a'}Q(s_{t+1},a')-Q(s_t,a_t)
\right].
$$

The behavior policy can explore.

The update target uses the greedy action.

This makes Q-learning off-policy.

See On-Policy vs Off-Policy.

heading: Why bootstrapping helps
text:
Monte Carlo methods wait for full returns.

TD methods update from one step.

TD targets have bias when values are imperfect.

They often have lower variance than full returns.

See Monte Carlo vs TD.

heading: Code example
text:
```python


q = np.zeros((n_states, n_actions))
alpha = 0.1
gamma = 0.99

def q_update(s, a, r, s_next):
    target = r + gamma * np.max(q[s_next])
    q[s, a] += alpha * (target - q[s, a])
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not call Q-learning on-policy.

Do not forget exploration during data collection.

Do not use a large step size with unstable function approximation.

heading: Overview
text: SARSA updates action values with the next action actually sampled by the behavior policy. It learns the value of the policy that it follows.

heading: Core idea
text:
SARSA stands for state, action, reward, next state, next action.

The update uses the tuple:

$$
(s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1},a_{t+1}).
$$

The update is:

$$
Q(s_t,a_t)
\leftarrow
Q(s_t,a_t)+\alpha
\left[
r_t+\gamma Q(s_{t+1},a_{t+1})-Q(s_t,a_t)
\right].
$$

heading: On-policy control
text:
SARSA is on-policy.

It evaluates and improves the same policy that collects data.

With an $\epsilon$-greedy policy, SARSA accounts for future exploratory actions.

Q-learning instead uses $\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$.

That difference can make SARSA more cautious in risky tasks.

See Q-Learning and TD Learning.

heading: Algorithm
text:
1. Choose action $a_t$ from the current policy.

2. Take the action.

3. Observe reward and next state.

4. Choose next action $a_{t+1}$ from the current policy.

5. Apply the SARSA update.

heading: Code example
text:
```python
def sarsa_update(q, s, a, r, s_next, a_next, alpha, gamma):
    target = r + gamma * q[s_next, a_next]
    q[s, a] += alpha * (target - q[s, a])
```

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not replace the sampled next action with a max action.

Do not call SARSA off-policy in its basic form.

Do not forget that exploration affects the learned values.

heading: Overview
text: Soft Actor-Critic trains a stochastic policy to maximize reward plus entropy. It is off-policy and uses replay for data efficiency.

heading: Core idea
text:
SAC maximizes a maximum-entropy objective:

$$
\mathbb{E}
\left[
\sum_t
\gamma^t
(r_t+\alpha \mathcal{H}(\pi(\cdot \mid s_t)))
\right].
$$

The entropy term rewards stochastic behavior.

The temperature $\alpha$ controls the entropy reward.

heading: Soft value target
text:
SAC uses a soft action value.

A common target is:

$$
y
=
r+\gamma
\left[
Q_{\bar\phi}(s',a')
-\alpha \log \pi_\theta(a' \mid s')
\right].
$$

The action $a'$ comes from the current policy.

Target networks stabilize the critic update.

heading: Actor update
text:
The actor minimizes:

$$
\mathbb{E}_{s,a \sim \pi_\theta}
[
\alpha \log \pi_\theta(a \mid s)-Q_\phi(s,a)
].
$$

This encourages high value and high entropy.

heading: Why SAC works well
text:
SAC is off-policy.

It can reuse replay-buffer data.

Entropy helps exploration and reduces premature collapse.

See Exploration vs Exploitation.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not drop the entropy term when describing SAC.

Do not forget target networks for stable critic training.

Do not assume SAC is on-policy.

heading: Overview
text: RL gradients often have high variance because rewards are noisy and delayed. Baselines, advantage estimates, bootstrapping, clipping, and normalization reduce variance.

heading: Core idea
text:
Policy-gradient estimates can vary greatly across trajectories.

High variance slows learning and can destabilize updates.

Variance reduction tries to make estimates less noisy.

Some methods keep the estimator unbiased.

Other methods add bias for lower variance.

heading: Baselines
text:
A baseline subtracts a value that does not depend on the sampled action.

The common choice is $V(s)$.

This gives the advantage:

$$
A(s,a)=Q(s,a)-V(s).
$$

The expected policy gradient stays the same.

The variance often becomes smaller.

heading: Reward and advantage normalization
text:
Many implementations normalize advantages in a batch:

$$
\hat A
=
\frac{A-\operatorname{mean}(A)}
{\operatorname{std}(A)+\epsilon}.
$$

This changes scale and can improve optimization.

It does not solve biased value estimates.

heading: Bootstrapping and GAE
text:
TD targets use bootstrapping to reduce return variance.

GAE mixes TD errors across multiple horizons.

The GAE parameter $\lambda$ controls the bias-variance tradeoff.

See GAE.

heading: Importance weight control
text:
Off-policy corrections can have high variance.

Clipping importance weights reduces variance.

It also adds bias.

PPO clips policy ratios for a related reason.

See PPO.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not assume lower variance always improves final performance.

Do not normalize rewards across tasks without checking meaning.

Do not use clipped weights without tracking the bias.

heading: Overview
text: A world model learns a compact predictive model of the environment. Dreamer trains an actor and critic on imagined rollouts in the learned latent space.

heading: Core idea
text:
A world model predicts how the environment changes.

It often uses latent states instead of raw observations.

A latent model can predict rewards, discounts, and future latent states.

Dreamer uses this learned model to imagine trajectories.

Then it trains the policy from those imagined trajectories.

heading: Dreamer components
text:
Dreamer has three main parts.

1. A representation model encodes observations into latent states.

2. A dynamics model predicts future latent states.

3. Actor and critic networks learn from imagined rollouts.

The model does not need to reconstruct every pixel perfectly.

It must predict information useful for control.

heading: Imagined rollouts
text:
Dreamer starts from real latent states.

It rolls the dynamics model forward under the actor.

It computes predicted rewards and values.

Then it updates the actor and critic through the imagined trajectory.

This improves data efficiency.

heading: Main risks
text:
Learned dynamics can be wrong.

Long imagined rollouts can compound model errors.

The policy can exploit mistakes in the model.

Short horizons and model regularization can help.

heading: Link to other methods
text:
Dreamer is model-based.

MuZero also plans in a learned latent space.

See MuZero.

heading: Common mistakes
text:
Do not require a world model to reconstruct raw observations.

Do not trust long imagined rollouts without checking model error.

Do not confuse latent dynamics with observed-state dynamics.
